subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, June 16, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one would indeed be insensible of feeling were he not moved by the applause which has just greeted him from all sides of the house as he rises in his first attempt in the role of so-called financial critic of the

government. I do most sincerely appreciate the generosity and the expression of goodwill of hon. members of this house.
It was with mixed feelings of gratitude and disappointment that I listened to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) deliver his budget the other day: gratitude to find that the minister had become converted to so many Conservative doctrines and policies, with which I will deal later, and disappointment to find no provision in that budget to give relief to the hard-pressed taxpayer of this country. The minister's diction was perfect, his articulation modulated, and I admired the agility of mind with which he could take a given set of facts and weave them into an argument to explain the prevailing conditions in this country, when in fact those very facts demonstrated clearly the shortcomings of this government to meet the needs of the people.
I do, however, congratulate the Minister of Finance on bringing down a budget at all. Most of us read in our school books the story of the Spartan boy who stood with stoical face while a wolf concealed beneath his clothes gnawed at his vitals. So long has the delivery of the budget been delayed this year that the business community has become very fearful that the wolf of the laissez-faire policy of this government had consumed the vitals of the government and that we would not have a budget at all. Every year preceding the delivery of the budget there is, for a few weeks, a slackening in business and industry because of the uncertainty of business men and industrialists as to the conditions under which they will have to carry on their business for the ensuing year by reason of tariff or taxation changes. This year that uncertainty has been emphasized and continued until it has grown into a major factor in the si owing-up processes of recovery which were going on in this country while the government was pursuing the mirage of a consummated trade agreement. Later on I shall have something to say with respect to the government's trade agreements.
The minister's explanation of the business decline in Canada during the past eight months or a year, with its consequent result of declining income, must have seemed naive to some of the Liberal members of this house. In order to convey to the country the idea that the policies of this government had saved the dominion from a recession to the same extent as that experienced by other countries, the Minister of Finance made this statement as reported at page 3893 of Hansard:
In the last four months of 1937, our nearest neighbour experienced a decline in business activity more drastic than that which followed

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
the collapse of 1929. World production, trade and prices have also declined but less rapidly than in the United States.
Then further on:
In December a moderate decline set in and by April-
That is, of 1938.
-the index of the physical volume of business in Canada was about 9 per cent below that for April, 1937.
I advanced that argument in this house in 1934 when the Conservative party was the government and the Liberal party was the opposition. It was in the budget debate. I compared the drop in the trade of the world and of the United States with Canada, having regard to the peak year 1929, and the year for which we then had statistics, 1933, and comparing the year 1929 with the year 1933 I pointed out to the house that whereas world trade had dropped 68 per cent, and whereas the trade of the United States had dropped 65 per cent, the trade of Canada under the then Conservative government had dropped only 62 per cent. That argument was derisively received by the members of the then Liberal opposition, and one need only read the pages of Hansard to ascertain their criticism of it. Well, what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. If the fact that Canada's business activities have maintained a higher level than those of the United States or the world during 1938 is attributable to the policies of the government in power in this country, then a similar condition which prevailed at the depth of the depression must be credited to the former Conservative government.
It was indeed a consolation to have the Minister of Finance at least converted to the views expressed by the Conservatives some years ago, but I should like to point out that if the policy of a government with respect to internal and domestic problems can make the country more resistant to world forces and conditions, then obviously trade agreements such as that made by Canada with the United States are not helpful in maintaining business activity and employment at a maximum level in Canada. The Liberal policy as advocated in the election of 1935 and as advocated by the Liberals when they were in opposition in this house from 1930 to 1935 was trade agreements and more trade agreements. According to the Liberals, our problems of unemployment and excessive taxation could all be solved if we but went out and made trade agreements, throwing open our domestic market to the different countries of the world. How well I remember the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) 51952-258
standing in his place in this house and condemning the then Conservative government for its alleged policy of economic nationalism. He told us not once but time and time again that our policy of economic nationalism would never solve the problems of Canada and that they would only be solved by trade agreements with the different countries of the world and with the United States in particular. Apparently the Minister of Finance has learned that in times of depression trade agreements are but as aspen reeds. I again quote his words from the budget speech which he delivered last Thursday, as reported at page 3894 of Hansard:
Export trade is the chief medium through which changes in economic conditions in other countries affect the Canadian economy. Up to August last business conditions throughout most of the world had been improving and the world price level had been rising.
Therefore I say that Canada's progress upward from the depths of the depression is attributable to the general advance in business conditions throughout the world and to the raising of the world price level. If further evidence be required, I quote again from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance at page 3897 of this year's Hansard:
All who have listened to this recital of the facts in connection with recent developments in our foreign trade will, I am sure, be impressed with how vulnerable our economy is to the impact of external influences, and there may also be some who will question the wisdom of any substantial reliance upon foreign trade. There is no doubt about the high degree of vulnerability in our position.
So we have the Minister of Finance admitting that if we are to seek primarily to trade our products with foreign countries rather than fabricate and consume them at home we shall be dependent upon conditions in those foreign countries for the maintenance of our internal economy and of our own standard of living. Surely that is heresy to the doctrines of Liberalism.
The Conservative party has never advocated that we in this land should be economic nationalists, but we have advocated that to the extent that it is possible to consume in our own domestic market the things which we can produce economically, that domestic market should be protected, and every producer and every manufacturer in Canada should have an equal opportunity to sell his products in his own home market. To the extent that we produce more than we can consume, Conservatives have advocated the negotiation of trade agreements whereby we might accept products of other countries which we cannot produce economically in exchange for the surplus of our own products. Thus

The Budget-Mr. Lawson

it will be seen that the Conservative policy lessens to the greatest extent the degree of vulnerability resulting from economic conditions in foreign lands, and provides, having regard to world conditions, a maximum of employment for Canadian workers in Canadian factories fabricating Canadian products, and a maximum price in our own markets for our own natural products.
The minister stated that the Canadian economy was not showing any weakness which required corrective processes during 1937. He based the statement on the fact that the rate of decrease in employment was not as rapid as the rate of decrease in the physical volume of business.- He said, as recorded at page 3898 of Hansard:
In each of the last two years I have had to refer to the failure of employment to keep pace with the striking gains in business activity and to point out that this was a condition usually met with in the early stages of recovery from business depression. I am therefore pleased to be able to report that during 1937 the increase in the volume of employment was for the first time since 1929 more rapid than the rise in industrial production, and also that since tire downward trend in business began last December employment has declined less rapidly than other business indices.
That condition does not reflect strength in the Canadian economy. Increase in employment always trails increase in business activity, and likewise decrease in employment always trails decrease in business activity. If the Canadian domestic market has a given consumption, the moment the goods of the Canadian manufacturer begin to be displaced in that market he does not immediately discharge his employees or some of them. He first endeavours to compete by increased production without increased cost of production, or alternatively he still hangs on producing goods for a while in the hope that the recession is only temporary. That is the reason why we did not feel the impact of the trade agreement made by this government with the United States in 1936. It was not until it got into full swing in 1937 that it began to affect our employment and our Canadian economy.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
My friends may laugh, but I will give some figures in a moment. When United States manufactured goods were first given greater opportunities in our domestic market our industrialists endeavoured to meet that competition. The lapse of some months having proven that they could not meet the competition, you have had for the last eight months or a year a constant slowing up of employment in industry, and that slowing up will continue and be accelerated

as the operation of the Canada-United States trade agreement becomes more effective. Already you have had a slowing up, as the minister pointed out the other day, the index of employment in this country on October 1, 1937, being 119-6 and on May 1, 1938, 111-5.
The foregoing leads me to a discussion of the trade agreements made by this government. The Minister of Finance has endeavoured to establish the paternity of this government for the empire trade agreements. Again I quote his words, as found on page 3925 of Hansard:
Since the present administration came into office, Canada has been a contracting party to the two most comprehensive trade agreements that have been concluded since the great war. Our agreement with the United States in 1935 and our agreement with the United Kingdom in 1937 resulted in the reduction of effective duties on a wide range of Canadian imports. They also secured the enlargement and consolidation of marketing opportunities for Canadian exports in the two biggest import markets of the world, which in the last calendar year took between them about eighty per cent of Canada's total exports.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It sounds pretty good.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It does sound good. But I propose for a few minutes to consider these two trade agreements, not as to their collective results, but as to the results which have flowed from each.
I have previously stated that the trade agreement made by this government with the United States is contributing to unemployment in this country. Now let me consider the figures in connection with the United States trade agreement. My recollection is that the trade agreement came into effect on January 1, 1936, and was adopted in this house in May of that year. Well, I take the exports from Canada to the United States, excluding gold, for the year ended March 31, 1937, and I find that they aggregate $364,354,990. Our exports to the United States for the next succeeding year, ended March 31, 1938, amounted to $343,250,669, a decrease of $21,104,321. Now let us look at our imports from the United States. For the year ended March 31, 1937, these imports amounted to $393,720,662. For the next succeeding year, ended March 31, 1938, they amounted to $487,328,980, or an increase of $93,608,318. In other words, while our exports to the United States decreased by $21,000,000 odd, our imports during the same period from the same country increased by $93,000,000 odd. If hon. members care to examine the book from which I obtained my figures, namely "The Trade of Canada, April, 1938." as issued by our own bureau of statistics, they will find an almost unbroken record for the last year, of our

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
imports from the United States increasing month after month. No wonder this government is struggling to make a new trade agreement with the United States to avoid the complete destruction of the Canadian market as a result of the last agreement they made with that country.
Now for a few moments let us turn to the empire trade agreements. I was unable to obtain from the bureau of statistics a compilation of figures for exactly the same period of time as those relating to the United States, but I got them to within a month of it. So the figures I am about to give end with the month of April in each year instead of the month of March. Our imports from the British Empire during the twelve months ended April, 1937, amounted to $201,539,570. and our imports for the next succeeding twelve months, ended April, 1938, amounted to $231,208,159. In other words during that year our imports increased by $29,668,589. Now let us look at our domestic exports to the British Empire. For the twelve months ended April, 1937, our domestic exports amounted to $502,290,701. For the twelve months ended April, 1938, they were $519,659,942, showing an increase in our domestic exports to the British Empire of $13,369,241. In other words, while our exports to the United States under the Canada-United States trade agreement decreased by $21,000,000 odd, our exports to the British empire increased by $13,000,000 odd. When one contrasts the benefit of the empire trade agreements to Canada with the detriment of the United States trade agreement, is it any wonder the Minister of Finance on behalf of the government refers to the empire trade agreement as "our agreement with the United Kingdom in 1937"?
The empire trade agreements were made originally by a Conservative government under the leadership of the present leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bennett), in 1932, for a period of five years. They were renewed by this Liberal government in 1937, without any substantial or material change in a single principle.

Having voted against
them in 1932.

The minister says "our
agreement with the United Kingdom in 1937." Shall I ever forget the attitude of the Liberal party in this house and this countiy at the time of the negotiation of the empire trade agreements? Do you remember how the Liberals derisively upbraided the present leader of the official opposition and referred to "blasting a way into the markets of the 51952-258J
world"? Do you recall how the leader of the official opposition was accused then of-driving a hard bargain, of lacking in patriot* ism because he asked from empire countries a quid pro quo for concessions in our tariff?; Shall I ever forget that in the final analysis every member of the Liberal party but one rose to his feet in this house and voted against the empire trade agreements? And now the: Minister of Finance boasts of "our trade agreement with the United Kingdom in 1937.",
A few moments ago I mentioned the; criticism levelled against the leader of the official opposition because he had bargained with the United Kingdom and British commonwealth countries in connection with the trade agreements. As I sat in my seat last. Thursday and listened to the words of the Minister of Finance I could hardly believe my ears, for this is what he said, at page 3925 of Hansard:	,
-"Canada cannot give to-day and bargain to-, morrow." It is even more true, Mr. Speaker, in tlie world as it is to-day that unilateral tariff reductions will not get the wider export markets which our products need and which the government is securing for them.
Surely this is complete conversion to Conservative doctrines and Conservative policies. The pages of Hansard are replete with declarations by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier that the policy of the Liberal party so far as empire countries are concerned is to make unilateral reductions in tariff and trust to the other commonwealth nations granting us corresponding benefits in their markets. How often have I sat in this house and listened to the present Prime Minister rail against the bargaining policy of the leader of the official opposition and the Conservative party; yet in this budget the official spokesman for the Liberal party says, "Canada cannot give to-day and bargain to-morrow." What? Desertion of unilateral tariff reductions? This is more heresy to Liberal doctrines and Liberal policies. It seems to me I have a recollection of a budget brought down by the same Minister of Finance in this house in 1930. My recollection is that Canada gave unilateral reductions in her tariff in favour of the United States, and this very same minister valiantly defended that action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is mistaken; it was the United Kingdom.
The Minister of Finance says "no."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was the United Kingdom, not the United States.

I think I understated it a little bit, because in addition to giving them
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

to the United Kingdom this country did give unilateral tariff reductions which applied not merely to the United States but to all countries. Can I for a moment forget cast-iron pipe and cut flowers? I heard that so often in the house I know it was a unilateral tariff reduction.
Long before I had personally met the Minister of Finance or had come under the influence of his urbane personality I had heard of him by reputation. I had heard of him as the great free trade Lochinvar who was coming out of the west to teach us of the east the economic doctrine of free trade, which was to sever all our chains of bondage to tariffs and bargaining trade agreements. Oh well, I suppose we of the Conservative party should be happy that the virtue of the Conservative policy has at last converted the Minister of Finance to a declaration that "Canada cannot give to-day and bargain tomorrow."
The minister told us when he came to the question of interest rates that the burden of interest upon the Canadian people had been reduced gradually by voluntary conversion operations resulting last year in a decrease of $5,592,000 in the amount of interest payable by the Canadian people. And he pointed out that by this method, as contrasted with an arbitrary cut in interest rates of 22^ per cent in Australia, Canada had benefited. The minister pointed out that the average rate of interest on Australian outstanding debt was decreased, by the arbitrary method adopted by them, to the extent of 25-1 per cent, while Canada's average interest rate, by reason of the voluntary method adopted by us, had been decreased by 29-1 per cent. In other words, the method of voluntary conversion and refunding was much more beneficial than the arbitrary method in relieving the taxpayer.
Again may I point out that this government is merely carrying out the policy inaugurated by the Conservative party, when we were in office prior to 1935. It was no easy task in those days for the former Conservative government to resist pressure from opposition members in the house, because we were in dark days of depression. The pressure brought to adopt the policy of arbitrarily cutting interest rates was very heavy. But let us not forget that it was a Conservative government which steadfastly refused to subscribe to a policy of repudiation, and to-day the people of Canada are reaping the benefit of that stand.
Let me for a moment or two turn to the tariff changes. The budget contains none.

At page 3925 of Hansard the minister is reported as follows:
For reasons which I believe will commend themselves to the house, I am not proposing any amendments to the customs tariff in the present budget resolutions.
I do not know whether the reasons for the failure to make tariff changes will commend themselves to the house, but I am pretty confident the reasons will not commend themselves to the people of Saskatchewan. I am confident the people of Saskatchewan will now come to the same conclusion as that to which many hon. members had previously come, that despite the injury which might be done to Canadian business by delay in bringing down the budget, this budget with no tariff changes in it would not be received until after the electors in Saskatchewan had gone to the polls.
I am sure the reasons will commend: themselves to the hon. Liberal member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) and to the hon. Liberal member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann), in view of the speeches they made in the house in favour of the maintenance of the tariff on agricultural implements and cream separators. But I wonder if the reasons will commend themselves to the hon. Liberal member for Lake Centre (Mr. Johnston) who, in advocating reduction in the tariff on agricultural implements, is reported as follows at page 1243 of this year's Hansard:
Serious consideration should be given to the matter of removing all duties on the general line of farm implements.
I am wondering if the reasons will commend themselves to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) who, speaking with respect to the tariff on agricultural implements, is reported to have said the following at page 2403 of this year's Hansard:
The present tariff of ?*} per cen,t is the lowest on record, if excise taxes and some other imposts put on through the regulations of the revenue department are not taken into account. But in the face of this reduction in the tariff we find the implement companies increasing their prices in 1936, and again in 1938. To me this looks like a challenge to the parliament of Canada. What are we going to do about it?
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance answers, "For reasons which will commend themselves to this house,"-nothing. . And again, the same hon. member for Portage la Prairie is reported in these words at page 2416 of Hansard:
We maintain that there is a great difference between the two old political parties on the tariff. The Conservatives stand for high protection. and the Liberals for low tariff; if there is no difference between a low tariff and a high tariff we should know it, and the way

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
to find out is to strip these companies who have defied parliament of all tariff protection, and let them stand on their own feet.
To the hon. member for Portage la Prairie this budget will be an awakening. Those of us who are on the Conservative side realized years ago that the Liberal party when out of power preached freer trade in western Canada and tariffs in eastern Canada, but that when in power it nibbled at the tariff a little bit here and a little bit there, with respect to certain industries, thus unbalancing the whole protective structure of the country.
I wonder if the reasons will commend themselves to the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) and the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver). The hon. member for Halton is reported at page 2611 of this year's Hansard as follows:
As to the 71 per cent duty on implements-
He was referring to agricultural implements.
-I would be quite content that it should be referred to the tariff board for hearing, but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the evidence would abundantly justify the entire removal of the duty.
Will the reasons commend themselves to the hon. Liberal member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) who said, as recorded at page 2571 of this year's Hansard:
And lastly, because of the monopolistic character of the industry, and also because the tariff is being belittled as a price-governing factor, the government should remove the duty and thus allow the freest competition possible so far as prices are concerned.
I wonder if the reasons will commend themselves to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Winkler) or to the hon. member for Dauphin Mr. Ward). The latter member is reported on page 2636 as having said with reference to the Minister of Finance:
I hope he will wipe out the duties on farm implements, and also on cream separators. I hope he will go a long, long way-as far as he has ever gone before-in reduction of tariffs.
What disillusionment there has been for the hon. member for Dauphin, and what a blight
to his hopes!
They will still vote for the budget.

Those are the truest words that ever were spoken. That interjection by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser) proves completely the point I made a few moments ago as to what they preach in the west and what they preach in the east. The hon. member interjects, "They will vote for the budget." Of course they will.
I cannot leave this subject without asking if the reasons will commend themselves to the
hon. Liberal member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), the former Minister of Agriculture in the Liberal government. He said, as is reported on page 2667 of Hansard:
I should judge from the speech of the Minister of Agriculture, however, that the interpretation thereof is that the government is considering the matter very carefully-
They were dealing with agricultural implements.
-and is evidently on the point of some important decision with respect to it.
Well, we have the important decision-do nothing. Is it any wonder that the electorate of this country is deceived when the former Liberal Minister of Agriculture cannot interpret clearly the words and policies of the present Liberal Minister of Agriculture?
No record in this matter would be complete without reference to the hon. Liberal member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). That pleasing and voluble gentleman has just returned to this house from his crusade in Saskatchewan on behalf of the provincial Liberal party.
Successful.

Yes, it was successful. L am ready to give him credit for that if you will just bide your time. The hon. gentleman returned with a fresh laurel wreath upon his brow. He made a plea to this Liberal government in connection with the tariff on agricuL tural implements. Let me read what is reported on page 2674 of Hansard of this year. He said:
I beseech the house to pass this report. I suggest that the government go further and take the duty off agricultural implements. They should then watch things very closely, and if prices do not come down at least to a figure comparable to prices in 1932,-
Mark you, that was when a Conservative government was in power.
-when costs were lower, other decisive action should be taken to see that justice is done to that fundamental industry which is now so depressed in this country, the farming industry.
I am afraid my hon. friend will have to doff his new laurel wreath, hie him back to the province of Saskatchewan and use all his eloquence and persuasion this summer to convince the electors of that province of the soundness of the commendable reasons of the Minister of Finance for not reducing the tariff on agricultural implements.
This budget is outstanding, not for what it contains, but for what it does not contain. No provision of any kind is made therein for the domestic policy, discussed by the Minister of Finance, which will create for Canada an internal economy capable of resisting in a
.4076
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

large measure the shook and impact of financial [DOT] ftnd economic conditions in other countries. It was at least gratifying to learn from the budget that the Minister of Finance realized that it was necessary to have a policy in respect to internal problems. I quote him again, as reported on page 3897 of Hansard:
A fundamental fact that in this modern world no nation can live unto itself alone does not lessen, indeed it reinforces, the necessity for Canada to devote its maximum energies to the solution of its own internal problems. Concentration upon its domestic problems is the primary duty of any nation.
Fine sounding words and a pious declaration ! What has this government done about it? The government has been in office three years. It has brought down three budgets. We are now at the end of the third session of this parliament, and what, I ask, has this government done to meet its primary duty of solving our domestic problems? The answer is-nothing, except a belated housing scheme brought down within the last three weeks, ; combined with an exemption from sales tax, provided in the budget, on the major commodities used in the building industry and even this scheme with respect to housing cannot become effective until the legislatures in the different provinces have met.
If I were to ask the women of this country, particularly the married women who have the responsibilities of a family, what they most desired in this life, I am confident that after mature consideration they would answer -security. They want security for the home; security for the job of the husband; security for a continuation of income into the home when the husband is out of employment; security for their children as to the possibility of profitable employment on attaining a working age. Surely that is a domestic problem which should be the primary duty of any government. What has this government done about ,it? Nothing.
If I were to ask the youth of this land what was their primary desire in life, I am confident that, after mature deliberation, they would answer-a chance, or an opportunity. They want a chance at a job; a chance to earn a living; a chance to marry; a chance to have a home; a chance for advancement in the social strata as a reward for merit. Surely the solution of that domestic problem is the primary duty of any government. What has this government done about solving that problem? Absolutely nothing, except a very limited yotith training project.
If I were to ask the farmers of this country what they most desire, I am confident they would answer-a steady market with a reason' /Mr. Lawson.]
able price level. Obviously you cannot give them a steady market with a reasonable price level by trade agreements, because then you are affected always by the conditions in foreign lands. The present operation and effect of the trade agreement made by this government with the United States conclusively proves the instability of a foreign market so far as maintaining prices in Canada is concerned. Foreign markets are all very well for our surplus products, but let the farmers of this country never forget that the finest market they will ever have, with the steadiest level of prices, is the hungry mouths of the city workers and factory toilers in this country, provided they have the pay envelopes from which to purchase farm products. What has the present government done to obtain for the farmer a steady market and a reasonable price level? Just nothing.
Supporters of the government will say to me-I am surprised that they have not already done so-"Well, what do you propose should be done to fulfil the primary duty of the government to the nation to solve its domestic problems?" I frankly admit that at this time and on this occasion, with a great Conservative convention to be held within two weeks which is to determine the policy of the Conservative party, I am not at liberty to enunciate a policy on behalf of the people of the Conservative party. But this I do say: if you are to give security to the women and the workers in this land, if you are to give an opportunity to youth, if you are to give a reasonably stable market with reasonably consistent prices to farmers, you must wipe out the growing spirit of provincialism and sectionalism in this country and you must obtain a maximum of cooperation between the provincial governments and this dominion government and a unity of purpose of the Canadian people.
During the campaign of 1935 I heard a great deal about the cooperation that this government was to obtain between the provincial governments and the dominion government if the Liberal party were returned to power. Need I quote the speeches of the present Prime Minister when he went about this country and said to the people, "You have a Liberal government in power in all the provinces but one, and if you elect a Liberal government to power in the dominion you will then have governments with common ideals and common policies; you will get a maximum of cooperation; we shall be able to sit around a table in conference and agree and find a solution of your problems." Well, were they able to obtain cooperation? Were

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
they able to obtain an agreement for the necessar, amendment to the British North America Act, which amendment could have preserved every minority right in this country and yet have allowed a national law for unemployment insurance, for minimum wages and for maximum hours of labour? They were not. Have they have been able to get cooperation from the Liberal government of Nova Scotia to facilitate the marketing of coal mined in that province, in the thickly populated centres of Ontario and Quebec? They have not.
They have.

No, they have not, if t'he hon. member will permit me. You have not *changed the statutes one whit since you came into office. Has this government been able to get cooperation with the Liberal government of the great industrial and agricultural province from which I come, the province of Ontario? So estranged is the government of that province from the government of the dominion that the Liberal premier of Ontario publicly declares that he is no longer a Mackenzie King Liberal. No, if cooperation is essential to the performance of the primary duty of any government to solve the country's domestic problems, it will never be accomplished by this government.
Now, in concluding, let us consider for a few minutes the financial aspect of this budget. Canada is labouring under a terrific burden of debt and taxation. If we add together the taxation imposed upon our people by the dominion, 'by provinces, by municipalities, by school boards and other taxing bodies, the figures which result are astronomical. I saw recently in some publication-I cannot vouch for the accuracy of the figures, but I believe they are correct-that out of a national per capita income of $347 a year in Canada the taxation by governmental bodies was $97 per capita. That means that 28 per cent of the per capita earnings of the Canadian people are paid in taxes each year. True it is that this dominion government cannot control the taxation of other taxing bodies, but surely this government can set an example and give encouragement to other taxing 'bodies by some effort at making tax reductions of its own.
One of the fourteen pledges of the present Prime Minister to the electorate in his campaign speeches of 1935 was that there would be retrenchment in public expenditure, a reduction of the principal of the public debt, and a reduction in taxation. What has the government done about it? Let us look at the record as shown by this budget.
According to the figures given us by the Minister of Finance, the total revenue
collected by this government in the last fiscal year is the largest ever collected by any government in this country in the same period of time. I want to compare the figures at the end of the fiscal year, March 31, 1938, with those at the end of the fiscal year, March 31, 1936. I pick 1936, Mr. Speaker, because this government was elected to power in October, 1935, and took office in November.
October.
Was it October or November, 1935?
October 23, 1935.

I do not think that they can be held accountable for any collection of taxes for the remainder of that fiscal year.
The total revenue collected by this government for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1938, was $516,692,000. Now let me take the corresponding figure for the last year in which the Conservative government was in office. The total revenue collected for the year ended March 31, 1936, was $372,596,000. The government collected last year in taxes-I should not have said, in taxes, 'but in revenue-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is better. .

-$144,096,000 more than the Conservative government in its last fiscal year of office, ended March 31, 1936. And the government tell us, according to this budget, that this year they will spend the vast sum of $530,000,000.
I gave the revenue from all sources. Let me now give the revenue from taxes collected by this government, and I take the same period of time. The revenue received by this government from taxes upon the people for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1938, was $448,652,000; the revenue collected from taxes for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1936, was $317,312,000. If you subtract one from the other you obtain the result that this government collected in taxes from the people for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1938, the sum of $131,340,000 more than was collected for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1936.
It means an increase in business.

I do not want to interfere with the continuity of my speech or I would answer the hon. member right now.
Not only has the government collected more taxes but it has spent more money. I wish to read a few figures, and to be fair I will omit from them all capital expenditures, all expenditures upon unemployment and agricultural relief. I find that the government spent in controllable expenditure for the fiscal
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

year ended March 31, 1938, $410,954,000 and that the ordinary expenditure, controllable, for the year ended March 31, 1936, was $372,-
539,000.	If you subtract one from the other you obtain the result that this government has increased controllable expenditure during the last fiscal year by $38,415,000; and yet in 1935 one of the fourteen points in the platform of the present Prime Minister was retrenchment in expenditures, reduction of the public debt, and reduction in taxation. Under this government, therefore, the people must struggle along with an ever-increasing burden of taxation.
And now I will answer my hon. friend who said that these increased taxes came from increasing business. Another promise in the Prime Minister's fourteen point program was reduction in the sales tax. In his campaign speeches the Prime Minister decried the fact that the sales tax had once been one per cent and that in 1935 it was six per cent, and he pledged his party, if it were returned to power, to decrease the sales tax. His exact words were that he would cut or drastically reduce the sales tax. Well, he fulfilled that pledge by increasing the sales tax the very first session his government was in power, increasing it from six per cent to eight per cent; and at eight per cent it still remains.
With a view to giving impetus to the building industry this budget exempts from the sales tax some of the principal products used in the construction of houses. That should prove a benefit to a part of the construction industry and I sincerely hope it will. But I will put this question to the Minister of Finance: If the abolition of the sales tax in respect of materials going into the building industry will give an impetus to the building industry, is it not obvious that a reduction in the sales tax would be a boon to industry in general? But it would be more than that. It would be a boon to every citizen in this land, because it would increase his purchasing power. Every time a man buys a dollar's worth of boots or clothing, or any other articles, food or necessities, more than eight cents of that dollar goes to this government in taxes because of the pyramiding of the sales tax.
I well recall how the Conservative government was condemned for imposing a sugar tax upon the people because it was said that it was a burden upon the poor. What has this government done about it? After three years of Liberal government, three budgets and three sessions, we still have the burden of the sugar tax upon the poor. I cannot refrain from reminding the house that during the campaign of 1935 the Conservative government

was upbraided from every platform for having put on an excise tax of three per cent. But after three years of this Liberal government, three sessions and three budgets, we still have the excise tax of three per cent. I can, however, hold out a hope to the Canadian people; I can hold out to the Canadian taxpayer the hope that this government, being compelled in the ordinary course of events to account to the electorate in 1939 and again to seek their votes, will reduce many of these burdens in the expectation of being able once more to delude the electorate with promises of a happy future.
As I pointed out a few moments ago, this government collected from the people of Canada in the last fiscal year $131,340,000 more in taxes than the Conservative government collected in its last year of office. This government has the doubtful honour of being the greatest tax collector in all the history of Canada since confederation. They are distinguished for the combination of a laissez-faire, do-nothing policy and the extraction from the people of Canada of the largest amount of taxes ever collected. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move:
That all the words after "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that the financial proposals submitted by the Minister of Finance for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1939, fail to make adequate provision for reduction of the excessive burden of taxation now borne by the Canadian people.

I desire to extend to my hon. friend the member for York South (Mr. Lawson) my congratulations on the speech which he has just delivered. He has followed the admirable tradition of the Conservative party which ever since confederation has presented its views with ability and steadfastness to the people of Canada. I am not quite certain whether a Conservative party needs a Liberal party, but I am absolutely positive that a Liberal party needs a Conservative party. I have always held to that point of view. And now I congratulate them again upon their having another convention in order to reorganize their party and do something better than they have done in the past. Years ago, as the date of a Conservative convention approached, I wrote an article in which I expressed my hopes for the prosperity of the Conservative party. I want to give the house to-day the first paragraph of that article, because history has a tendency to repeat itself, and the words I then wrote need only one change, the substitution of Ottawa for Winnipeg as the place of the convention:

The Budget-Mr. Deachman
Not for worlds would I attempt to call the dead to life for vain purposes. A Conservative party has a place in Canada. Breeching is needed in a set of harness as well as tugs-a fish line has a sinker as well as a cork. Lloyd George remarked not long ago that every man has a little House of Lords in his own mind. So long as Conservative instincts survive there will be need for a Conservative party. We cannot have joy without sorrow, the lilt of laughter without a background of tears, or pleasure without pain. When Conservatism dies Liberalism may prepare its own epitaph. All good Liberals should pray for the success of the Winnipeg convention. Liberalism in Canada needs a Conservative party. It needs something on which it may sharpen its weapons -better far that Liberals should be temporarily submerged in an open fight, with sword in hand and visor down, than that it should pass out in the inglorious occupation of twiddling its thumbs.
Having listened to our distinguished friend this afternoon, I would say there can be no possibility of death by that route. We have in the Conservative party one leader at least who stands by the old traditions. His attitude to-day was perfect. It was the same remedy as was offered in 1878; it was 1930 repeated over again; it was emphasis piled on emphasis to suggest that what this country needs is more conservatism, more high tariffs, reliance upon our home market, development of our home industry, and nothing else.
The hon. member spoke of our vulnerability, from the trade standpoint, our danger from outside nations. He thought invulnerability would be secured if we piled our tariffs high enough. I wonder if he happens to recall the existence of a nation called the United States of America. It is a near neighbour of ours, and is sometimes quoted in Conservative literature. Does he recall the fact, which I think I have mentioned once before in this house, that in the campaign of 1930 the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in one of his great efforts referred to the progress of the United States, and said: We see her now marching forward to the tune of America first; and then a few short months later the only tune heard across the line was: Brother, can you spare a dime? I wonder if he recalls that when the depression came, the United States of America was the first to face the crash. We passed through a period of depression, moved upward in the scale towards a greater measure of prosperity, and then there came another recession or depression. Who led in that downward march? Again the United States of America. It had placed its reliance upon tariffs; it had built for invulnerability and made itself the most vulnerable nation in the world. I wonder whether, looking over the map of Europe to-day, he will recall that the peoples with the highest tariffs are the peoples who are now under
despotisms-a natural and obvious route, inescapable, because the removal of tariffs raises the standard of living, and when the standard of living sinks below a certain level there is a tendency to revolt and to try something else. So some of the greatest protectionist nations, frequently pointed to in the past as among those which had made the most progress under protection, now stand,-as Germany and Italy, unable to carry on a democratic government, facing difficulty and creating a strong disturbing influence in the world.
The hon. member referred to the development of home industry, his main argument for protection, I propose to cite the income of the Dominion of Canada at the present time; and no matter what has happened, the income seems to be doing fairly well. In 1930 the total income of the Dominion of Canada was 5,173 millions of dollars. In that year the Liberals of Canada went out of office because the income was not large enough. The Conservative party came in, and the income dropped to a low level of 3,193 millions of dollars in 1933. When I hear a speech such as that delivered by my hon. friend this afternoon I wonder why in those solemn years he did not call upon his gods to arrest the decline of two billion dollars in income in those three years. If a high tariff means something, why did the tariff not work? I wonder what, was the reason. Yet I got a suggestion of a possible answer from my hon. friend this afternoon. He told us that it took some time for the reduction in tariffs against the United States to work an injury to the people of Canada. At the same time he thought it took three or four or five years before the new gospel of high and higher protection, the Conservative doctrine, would relieve the situation which then existed. Well, in 1935 there was a change of government. The income that year was 4,094 millions of dollars. I have these figures from the bureau of statistics to-day. It went up in 1937 to 4,870 millions, an increase in the national income between 1935 and 1937 of 776 million dollars. I am not anxious to claim the credit for the Liberal government for all of that increase. I believe in making the statement as fair as possible. I have a suspicion that in this house, on rare occasions, both parties claim credit for things for which they were not wholly responsible. But when I have shown the decline of income under the Conservative policy of high protection, and the increase under a Liberal administration, at least you cannot logically decide that it would be the part of wisdom to have a higher tariff than we have. We have done better since reductions have been made, relatively small as, in my humble judgment,
The Budget-Mr. Deachman

these reduction have been; I am also going to suggest later that they ought to have been greater.
Now my hon. friend says that we need a steady market, and that that market can be built up at home. What you need, he says, is the hungry mouths of the workers in the factories to provide the market. But the trouble is that under Conservative administration the mouths were too hungry and the difficulty was to satisfy the hungry by giving employment. We have changed and improved that since we have adopted a different policy, and have once more started on the upgrade.
My hon. friend referred to the position of the farmer. I am particularly interested in this subject, and I want to point out precisely what has happened. I should like my Conservative friends, if they are in the house now, to listen to these facts, which record the actual transposition which has taken place between 1930 and 1937. In 1930 it took 106 units of farm products to buy a dollar's worth of manufactured goods. Then the Conservative party came into power. The following year it took 132 units. They were not doing too badly for the manufacturers, were they? In 1933 it took 144 units, the next year 137 units and in 1935 it took 124 units. When the Liberals came into office it took 114 units; in 1936 it took 106 units; and in 1937 farm products and manufactured products were back upon a basis of parity of exchange. You could take 100 units of farm products and exchange them for 100 units of manufactured products. Yet my hon. friend from York South suggests that the sober, thoughtful farmers of the Dominion of Canada, looking at these facts and considering not only their own interests but the interests of the nation, should crawl back under the banner of Conservatism under which they lost their income and were reduced to lower levels than at any previous time in the history of Canada.
Then my hon. friend suggested that there had been an increase in expenditure during the last year and that we had taxed the people of Canada more than we did previously. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is the old story; with business expanding more revenue was collected. I suggest that you look back once more at the position of the farmer; when he was paying 144 units of farm products for 100 units of manufactured products he was not in a position to buy a very large volume of goods in the open markets of this country. But without any change whatever in taxation a point of equality was reached as between manufactured and farm products, and what followed? The farmer was able to buy more manufactured goods; there was more employment in the cities. The farmers, having a larger avail-

able sum with which to buy products in the markets of the world, purchased them, so that revenues from the tariff, from the sales tax and from all other impositions steadily moved upward. More revenue was collected because of the greater capacity of the people to buy goods, yet you have the challenge thrown out by the Conservative financial critic to-day that we increased the taxes on the Canadian people. In point of fact the prosperity of the Canadian people increased under a more Liberal policy than had existed previously, and with that increase in wealth came greater capacity to pay and therefore larger revenues. Well, I see no hope for anything so far as my hon. friend is concerned. He has nothing to suggest. In his opinion it is simply the old, old story of higher and higher peaks of taxation, more and more tariffs and relatively less revenue.
Now, passing from my hon. friend from York South, I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon at least one thing in his budget, a feature which under his administration has been greatly developed. In this connection I do not desire to withhold credit from some of the Conservative financial leaders as well; but this year, as last year, my hon. friend presented a budget that was very simple, very clear and very direct. It is quite possible for any ordinary man to understand it, and I only wish every province in Canada and, indeed, every financial institution would adopt a similarly clear method of presenting their stories so that the man on the street, the man in parliament, the leader of thought and opinion, would be able to get a clear understanding of the financial situation. Then there would be less lax thinking. Not many years ago I heard three cabinet ministers state the amount of the debt of the Dominion of Canada, and each gave a different figure. If it is possible for men trained as they were to give different figures in regard to a simple matter of that kind, what about the ordinary man who has only an occasional opportunity to read these things and who therefore lacks the training that would enable him to understand them?
I want also to congratulate the Dominion of Canada, because I think the budget speech revealed the amazing capacity of the dominion to come back after such disasters as those through which we have passed. I wonder what any man standing here in 1914, when we had an export trade of $455,000,000, would have thought if it had been suggested that within four years our export trade would rise to over $1,500,000,000? I wonder what he would have thought if someone had said that within that time we would send five hundred thousand

The Budget-Mr. Deachman
men to the field of battle. Yet after the war, after a peace that was worse than war and after fiscal policies which were worse than the peace, we have survived and in 1938 have an [DOT]export trade of over a billion dollars. Sometimes we are too much in the habit of speaking of our export trade in terms of dollars. If we consider the physical volume we find that between the depths of the depression in 1933 and 1937, which is the last year for which I have the physical volume of business, there has been an increase of 47 per cent in the export trade of the dominion. And this was accomplished in a period during which drought interfered with the development of [DOT]our export markets. From the standpoint of bushels our wheat exports declined approximately 58 per cent. From the standpoint of dollars the difference between the average for the periods 1926-29 and 1935-38, in our exports of grain and flour, amounts to almost $300,000,000 a year. A country which can face losses and disasters such as these, at least part of which arose from no fault of its own, and can do it after it has suffered restrictive tariffs such as were imposed in the five years which followed 1930, must be a nation of striking force, a nation of which we may well be proud. It has shown the ability to suffer those setbacks and come back in a way that probably no other nation in the world could come back. Confucius, the great Chinese philosopher, once remarked that man's greatness is shown not in never falling but in rising every time he falls. I think the same might be said of a country. A nation shows its capacity by its ability to come back, by its resiliency, by its power to recover, and in that regard Canada stands out as a leader among the nations of the world.
These things are matters of encouragement, but there is always a serpent or two in the garden of Eden. The return to normal production has not given us the volume of employment which might be desired. There is no question whatever but that there is maldistribution of income in Canada. In part that is due to the destruction of our agricultural production by drought and also to the wide spread which I quoted a few moments ago as between agricultural and manufactured products. I want to give the figures, because I think this is something the house ought to consider; and I do not give them in any partisan sense. I deplore the tendency to place party above everything, and to try to create the impression that Conservatives or Liberals alone are perfect. There is a problem here which is too big for that, and I ask hon. members if possible to separate the political from the economic aspect, and to
listen for a moment to what has happened in Canada, to	that	which representsthe problem of the	people	of Canada. And whether it be Tory, Grit, C.C.F. or Social Credit, unless you reach the bottom of this problem you still leave the future of Canada in a position which to say the least is insecure indeed.
The year 1926 is generally considered the base year in Canadian statistics. I should like to place on record the money income in that year in different sections of Canadian industry, and then to place opposite it the real income. Because the money income expresses only the amount of dollars received, whereas the real income represents the amount of actual purchasing power which the people in different forms of employment receive for their work.
In the period 1931-35 the total wages in manufacturing industries was 16-8 per cent less than in the year 1926. But because of the difference in the cost of living the real wage, or the purchasing power of wages paid in Canadian industry, in the average year of 1931-35 period, was 2-3 per cent more than it was in 1926. Per capita money wages fell 9-7 per cent, whereas in real wages they were up 8-9 per cent. The share of capital-and by that I mean the amount left after deductions for salaries, wages and raw material- the sum out of which it had to pay interest, overhead and profit was 11-2 per cent below the 1926 level, in terms of money income, but was 9-5 per cent more in terms of real income.
I should like to point out that in those three, namely total wages paid, per capita wages and the share which went to capital in Canadian industry, there was a decline in money income, but an increase in real income during the period of the depression, as compared with the year 1926.
Now let me give the other side of the story. While those people were prospering there were some others who were not doing so well. I submit this fact, that you cannot have one-half of the people slaves and the other half free. I mean you cannot have one-half of the Canadian people cared for in a period of depression, while leaving the other half to chance. Raw materials declined in money value. This item represents raw materials used in Canadian industry, and therefore includes a certain percentage of imported products. Those who were selling raw materials got 32 per cent less money for them, and in real value received 17 per cent less than in 1926.
The share received by agriculture was 49 per cent below the amount received in 1926,
The Budget-Mr. Deachman

but the real income in agriculture fell by 36 per cent. Railway earnings, expressed in terms of money income, dropped 38 per cent, and in real income 23-6 per cent. Railway wages and salaries were 30'5 per cent lower, but expressed in terms of real income were 14-8 per cent lower. The per capita income received by the railway workers declined 6-3 per cent in money income, but was increased 15'4 per cent in purchasing power.
The problem I place before the house is a simple one. What are we going to do with the problem embodied in this small statement of facts? Is the House of Commons going to say, "All is for the best in the best of all possible worlds," when we find that during the five years of depression the burden fell upon the basic producer, and the farmer? So far as industry was concerned, the burden fell upon the railways, and that is the reason for our railway problem to-day.
That was the condition, while certain other classes in the community received fair recompense for the services they rendered. I have no panacea for these problems, but I do say that the House of Commons ought to consider them. I venture the further suggestion that if we are going to maintain the tariffs of to-day, which are lower than the tariffs of 1935, we will have to face the problem in an intensified form in the years which are to come, and the challenge made then will be keener than the challenge made to-day. We still have hopes. We who hold the view that the Liberal party will go forward with the expansion of markets, the reduction of tariffs, the idea of equality of opportunity for the different classes in the dominion and an enlarged opportunity for youth-as my distinguished friend would put it-we still have hopes!
It is sometimes said that in connection with these matters I am somewhat extreme- that is the word. I like to hear that. Well, I will venture to prove that I am not extreme. I want to show to the house not only that I am not extreme but that there are a few hon. members, on both sides perhaps, who in these matters are extreme, if there is any possibility of defining that term. For years, as many hon. members know, I appeared before the tariff board representing the Consumers' League. I asked for reductions in tariff, but never once in that period did I ever ask for a reduction in tariff below the wage content of the product produced.
Taking the census of industry for 1936 we find that total wages paid out in Canadian manufacturing industry represented 14-6 per cent of the value of the products produced. Salaries constituted 5-7 per cent. The average

rate on dutiable imports into this country in. 1936 was 26-7 per cent. If imports come from foreign countries outside the British Empire-they are subject to a 3 per cent excise tax, and that 3 per cent is applied to the duty paid value. Therefore one has to add 3-8 per cent to the 26-7 per cent. Then we have the sales tax, and the sales tax must be applied on the-duty, because the tax upon a duty is an added duty. Adding these we find a total of 32-8 per cent representing the average tariff in Canada on dutiable goods. In those goods we have a wage content of 14-6 per cent. Am I extreme when I say a tariff rate of more than twice the value of the wage content in the product, and one which represents more than 50 per cent in excess of the entire wages and salaries, is too high a tariff for Canada, and something which calls for a sharp reduction?
Let me put this before you in another way. You have a factory in which you are manufacturing goods. You produce one million dollars' worth of goods in a year. Your wage bill is . less than $150,000. If you import the products which are manufactured in that factory, under a Liberal government you would pay 32-8 per cent or $328,000. Is it enough? Well, I venture to suggest that it is substantially lower than it was under the Conservative government, but to me that is scant consolation. It is substantially higher than it was under the former Liberal government. I believe as Liberals that we should do something to get back to the days when we had a measure of freedom and when trade was not restricted as it is to-day.
Let us apply this to textiles. In 1930 the average rate on dutiable textiles from the United Kingdom was 20-3 per cent, leaving out the sales tax. excise tax and all those other things. In 1935 it was 29-3 per cent and in 1937, the average rate was 26-1 per cent. That is a reduction of a little over three per cent from the top level of 1935. The average rate on dutiable goods from foreign countries was 28-9 per cent in 1930, 36-6 per cent in 1935 and 34-8 per cent in 1937. I submit that those rates are too high and that something ought to be done about them. I am not an extremist when I point out these things to the house. I am a Liberal and I am simply calling attention to rates which are too high. Unless these rates are remedied they will not only destroy the industry of the dominion but will bring about a tragedy almost as great, the destruction of liberalism itself.
Here are some other rates which I am sure will be interesting to some of my hon. friends. I have taken the average rates on art silk from four countries, and it will delight

The Budget-Mr. Deachman
the hearts of Conservatives to know that these are countries with which we have favourable balances of trade. Here is the way we have used them in the last few years. The average rate on art silk imported from Belgium, [DOT]China, Italy and Japan is 103 per cent, not including excise tax, sales tax and other taxes. Am I an extremist when I point out these things? I contend that I am only a rationalist trying to argue what is sound and reasonable in a world which has gone tariff mad. But I have substantial support for my argument. I should like to quote one or two distinguished gentlemen. Sir Arthur Salter, in his book entitled World Trade and its Future, makes the following statement which has particular reference to the difficulty which we face in Canada to-day:
Always, as the negotiations proceeded, one felt that the dominant consideration in the mind of each national representative was not a conception of his nation's interests as a whole, mistaken or not, but a calculation of pressures to which the national government would be subjected by organized interests in the respective parliaments.
In other words, we are not suffering to-day from these extreme tariffs because the leaders *of thought and opinion want them. We are not suffering because the people of the Dominion of Canada or the people of the world want them

they do not. We are suffering because of the pressure brought to bear by definite groups upon the parliaments of almost [DOT]every country in the world. These groups, pressing their will persistently and steadfastly, deny to the people of the world the opportunity to come into the inheritance which is theirs. Sir Arthur goes on to say:
Consequently the net result of the Genoa resolutions was rather to endorse and consolidate a system of trade barriers which *everyone, looking at it as a whole, recognized to be injurious to world recovery, and those passages in them which recommended reductions remained as merely pious hopes without practical effect. And in general this was the *experience of other conferences of this period, though a few organized at Geneva for more modest and specialized purposes secured the removal of some of the least defensible forms [DOT]of trade obstruction.
I come now to the argument made by another distinguished gentleman. I quote from the report of the imperial economic conference of 1932. At that conference the present right hon. leader of the opposition had this to say:
When we reach an agreement-
He was referring to the empire agreements.
-by which our products pass more freely from one empire country to another, we drive clear channels through the stagnant pools dammed up by the world upheaval, and naturally we wil] carry past the boundaries of the empire
and to its benefit, establish once more again throughout the world that commerce which is its very life blood.
I heard the hon. member for York South tell us that what we needed was a more or less self-contained economy, one in which we could be free from contact with the outside world. We were to be made invulnerable, but we' have the leader of the Conservative party, the Prime Minister of that time, telling the assembled delegates that the way of escape was not by restriction, but by breaking down these barriers and restoring a larger measure of freedom of trade within the countries.
I regret to state that the hon. member's time has elapsed.
Go on.
It must be with the unanimous consent of the house.

I come now to another point. I only want to show the unity of thought that exists among men of different political beliefs and diversified thought. First I quoted the words of Sir Arthur Salter. Then I quoted my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. I should like now to quote the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). At the special session of 1930 he moved the following resolution:
This house regrets that the government has seen fit at a special session called to deal only with unemployment to propose great increases in customs taxation on a wide range of commodities under circumstances which prevent this house and the country from securing adequate information regarding the proposals and prevent proper parliamentary discussion of them.
In the opinion of this house the tremendous increases in taxation proposed will not end unemployment,

They did not.
-but will inevitably increase the cost of living-
They did not increase the cost of living very materially, but they increased it above what it would have been if greater freedom of trade had been given to us. I continue:
-and will also increase the cost of production in the primary industries, agriculture, fishing, mining and lumbering, thus making it more difficult for Canadian producers in these industries to meet world competition in marketing their products.
I have quoted the attitude of certain leaders of thought in the Dominion of Canada and elsewhere. I find myself in exact agreement with their views. Why should I be regarded as an extremist when I say that we should do these things? Why should anyone say that I am. an extremist when I accept the policy
The Budget-Mr. Deachman

which these men accept? Why should I be called an extremist for thinking as does every leader of thought, not only in the dominion but throughout the world? These are important things and things which should be considered very carefully in the present disturbed condition of the world.
I want to turn to one other matter. At the present time the members of the government are faced with a difficulty. They are trying to do something which beyond question ought to be done. They are trying to break down the barriers of trade. I confess that I do not hold with the convictions which the Minister of Finance has expressed in regard to unilateral tariff reductions. I hold to another view. I believe that tariff reductions aside from treaties should be made. It depends, of course, on the way that they are carried out. We are confronted with great difficulties in that regard. But if it can be successfully done, and if this proposed agreement becomes a broad measure, leading to a wide reduction among these nations and carrying through to, others by means of the most favoured nation treaties-if that is accomplished, beyond doubt it will be the greatest economic event of the present century. I do not think there is a doubt that it can be done, and if this government will bring it about, then indeed the Minister of Finance will have accomplished something which is an important Canadian event and an important world event.
We have reached a stage in world history when, I venture to suggest, no longer can any country in the world have a high standard of living and at the same time maintain a high tariff. I will give one example. Take a country like Baffin Land, whose population consists entirely of Eskimos, producing nothing but sealskins and blubber. They can have a comfortable standard of living, within their own conception of a standard of living, consisting of sealskins and blubber. They may have a national policy and vote for blubber and protection. But if they want to enlarge their standard of living they must market the products which they produce-exchange them for the products of other countries. I move from Baffin Land to Saskatchewan. The main products of that province are cattle and wheat. The people cannot live upon a high standard on cattle and wheat alone, so if they are to increase their standard of living they must provide a measure of freedom of exchange; they must have an opportunity to exchange the products they produce for the products which other people produce. Exactly the same state of

things, in varied measure, exists so far as the people of Ontario or the maritimes or British Columbia or any other province are concerned. If you would increase your standard of living you must have greater freedom of trade.
What does an increase in the standard of living mean? It means only one thing-the maintenance of high wages or a greater purchasing power; and when you restrict your trade by tariffs you are in fact voting for nothing else than a reduction in your real wages.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I am reluctant to interfere with an interesting speech, but I think it is a very early stage in the debate to establish the principle of unduly extending, beyond the conclusion of the point being made by your honour, the time allotted to the hon. member speaking.

I myself raised the point a few minutes ago, but all hon. members seemed anxious to hear the hon. member for Huron North speak somewhat longer, and that is why I allowed him to proceed. As a rule, hon. members should speak no longer than forty minutes.
Question.

I must say I regret that the hon. member did not conclude his speech in this debate. It was the latter part of his speech in which, I think, many of us were particularly interested.
I would join with those who have congratulated the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the manner of his presentation of the budget, the comprehensive survey which he has made. Congratulations should also be extended to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson), who made an excellent criticism of the minister's speech. And of course we always listen with a great deal of interest when the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Beachman) explains his views on tariff and financial matters.
In the budget speech and in the budget there was one particular thing which stood out very clearly, namely, that a vast proportion of our revenue is raised by taxes which bear heavily on the great masses of the people. We find, for example, that by way of customs import duties we collected $93,456,000; from the sales tax, $138,054,000, and from excise duties, $52,037,000, a total of $283,547,000. If, in addition, taxes on manufacturers' importations are added-and they ought to be because they are passed on to the consumers-we must add another $42,765,000,

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
making a grand total of $326,312,000. Now, break this down, as the minister did in his budget speech, on a percentage basis, and we find that customs duties account for 17'62 per cent of the revenue; sales tax, for 26-03 per cent; excise tax, for 9-81 per cent, making a total of 53-46 per cent for those items. If, as I contend we should, we add the manufacturers' importations, another 8-06 per cent, we have a total of 61-52 per cent of the entire revenue from import duties, sales tax and excise, an enormous percentage taken directly from the consuming masses of this country. It should be pointed out that these items together account for nearly $30 a head for every man, woman and child in Canada. When we remember that members of the Liberal party in this house from time to time have criticized and taunted our social credit friends because they have not carried out their promises, let us also remember that the Liberal party has not carried out its promises by reducing these important items which bear so heavily upon the masses of the people. Calculated on the basis of a family of five persons, it means that approximately $150 a year or $12.50 a month per family is collected in these hidden taxes, to say nothing of the exactions which are permitted by the operations of a tariff. That in itself would account for more than $25 per month per family, an amount of which we have heard so much . in the house during this session.
All we get in the budget besides the exemption from sales tax of building materials is an exemption from sales tax of food for fur-bearing animals, repairs for fishermen's boats, harness and harness parts, and gopher poison. The fox farmer gets his feed, the fisherman get his tar, and the prairie gopher gets his poison free of all sales tax. That is about all we have in the budget for these particular classes. What a commentary, I may add, on the budget of 1938!
The minister said that almost half of our total imports come into Canada free of duty. But when we examine that statement we find that these are mainly raw materials or partly manufactured articles for manufacturing industries. Then, of course, we find included the $100 exemption for tourists returning to this country. May I say here, because I wanted to say it earlier in the session, that when the department interprets the word "included" as "contained" in relation to that exemption, in my opinion they are misinterpreting the will of parliament.
After the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) had argued, in a discussion which occurred quite early in the session, that articles brought into this country must be "contained" in the baggage of the tourist, I looked into
the matter and found that the resolution of parliament used the words, "included in the baggage", which, it will readily be seen, is a very different matter.
As I listened to the first half of -the minister's speech I realized that it was an apology for the announcement which was to follow, the announcement of a policy of doing nothing; this conclusion was irresistible. My mind went back to those days when I listened to the Minister of Finance as a crusader for something approaching universal free trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He still is.
Then it is very carefully concealed in this budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Universal free trade
would be an admirable thing.

But in those days, I would point out, it was not only universal free trade, because in common w-ith many of us in western Canada, the hon. gentleman was preaching free trade as an economic and social philosophy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not for Canada alone, never.
Then I greatly misunderstood the minister, as many thousands did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman certainly did. He cannot quote a single speech of that kind emanating from me.

That was the interpretation we placed upon the minister's speeches in those days. If not the Minister of Finance, then to the left of him sits the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar).
