I remember repeating many of the arguments he used in the elections in the old days in the province of Saskatchewan from the platforms of the Progressive party of which he was at that time the leader.
Is that an argument for free trade?
No; but I remember the arguments which were used by the minister at that time in favour of free trade.
As a matter of fact my hon. friend, in many admirable speeches he made then, never argued for free trade.

I repeated many of the arguments of the minister, and I thought at that time I was arguing for free trade, but I find that I was probably in error. And of course I can remember the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), who was regarded as a convinced free trader in those days. Yet
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

to-day we have the Minister of Finance repeating with even greater emphasis what he said last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Two years ago.

I quote:
It is even more true, in the world to-day, that unilateral tariff reductions will not get the wider export markets which our products need and which the government is securing for them.
How, then, does this policy differ from that of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett)* who declared in 1930 that he would make the tariff work for Canada? He merely put the same thought more dramatically when he said, "I will blast my way into the markets of the world." The Minister of Finance went on to say:
The United States is not prepared to reduce its tariffs except by way of trade agreements, and the United Kingdom is now pursuing a similar policy.
Then he concludes that unilateral action by Canada is out of the question and that bilateral trade agreements form the policy of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What would my hon.
friend suggest should be done when two customers who take eighty per cent of all we have still definitely have that policy?
That was also true in 1930.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Britain was free trade in 1930.
Britain was free trade in 1930 only to a certain extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Entirely.
And she was rapidly going in the direction of a very low tariff, because the British tariff to-day is not comparable with the high tariff which we have in Canada at the present time.
And she was taking our products.

Yes. I am reminded that she was taking our products. But the point I make is this: How does this policy differ from the brick-for-brick policy which I am sure I heard the Minister of Finance denounce in western Canada some years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Well, to-day we are told that we cannot take off a brick unless the
[Mr. Coldwell.)
United States takes off a brick; and if on the other hand the United States puts a brick on we, too, by the same argument, should put a brick on. That would be a bilateral agreement to the fullest extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are saying that, not I.
That would be a countervailing duty.

Yes. I think, however, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) covered that point very well to-day. But where are all the Liberals who told the Canadian people of the wicked exactions that were taken through the tariff by the textile industry, the agricultural implement industry and other industries throughout Canada? Where, now, are the threats that were made a few weeks ago in this house by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and by others to the farm implement industry? That was before the Saskatchewan election, and those speeches, may I say, were widely circulated during that election. I have on my desk before me the manifesto of the premier of Saskatchewan in which he makes this statement regarding farm implements:
With the object of reducing the retail price, the government will continue to press upon the federal government the necessity of removing all tariff duties on farm implements. Should such action fail to bring about reasonable reduction the government will further press the federal government to take the necessary action to control the prices of such implements.
There we have a Liberal government in the prairie provinces within the last two weeks promising to use its influence, not for bilateral trade agreements, but for unilateral action, the removal of all tariffs from the farm implement industry. An hon. member suggests that he did not have enough influence. Well, statements of this description at any rate secured for the Liberal party in that province a goodly number of votes, and that, I think, is one factor which is undermining our democratic institutions at the present time. Political parties seek office on specific promises, and then, when they have achieved office, forget all about the definite pledges they have made.
The minister says that unilateral action cannot be taken. Such a statement is as old as the tariff controversy itself. As a matter of fact, the assertion that free trade depends upon its mutuality has always been the favourite argument of high protectionists. Give us universal free trade, they have always said, and we shall always be in complete accord with it. Protectionists have always argued that mutuality must be the key-note of free trade. Every book that I have read on the philosophy of free trade makes that particular point quite

The Budget-Mr. Caldwell
clear. I have heard hon. gentlemen opposite assert that countries which tax our exports to them not only injure us but injure world trade generally. I have heard them further say that every tariff wall is a wall not only against income but against outgo. That has been the argument used by our free traders throughout Canada, and indeed throughout the world-I was going to say, from time immemorial, but that would not be correct- for a century, ever since Cobden and Bright went on the war-path in favour of free trade in Great Britain.
Now a Liberal Minister of Finance says that tariff reductions will not get the wider export markets which our products need.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The hon. member has left out a word, the word "unilateral."

I am sorry; it was not intentional. Unilateral tariff reductions will not get the wider export markets which our products need. There we have a statement which has been made by every protectionist philosopher who has written a book on tariffs and protection. That is the reason why I said at the very outset that there seemed to be a considerable change in the outlook of the Minister of Finance from the days when I used to vote for him, incidentally, in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only very incidentally.
Oh, I have done it.

And you do not
regret it.

No, I do not regret it. How many Liberals in this house actually believe in the Liberal platform and are prepared to practise what that platform preaches? I should like to find out, and I think the country generally would like to find out. I therefore propose to move an amendment to the amendment, in which I have incorporated the Liberal tariff platform. I move, seconded toy Mr. Douglas (Weyburn):
That the amendment be further amended by adding the following thereto:
That this house further regrets that the proposals submitted by the Minister of Finance on June 16 disregard the pledges of the Liberal party to the Canadian people contained in its platform of 1919 and subsequent years, which declared, among other things, that the best interests of Canada demand that substantial reductions of the burdens of customs taxation be made with a view to the accomplishing of two purposes of the highest importance: first, diminishing the very high cost of living which presses so severely on the masses of the people; second, reducing the costs of the instruments 51952-259
of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the dominion, the vigorous development of which is essential to the progress of our country.
That to these ends, wheat, wheat flour and all the products of wheat, the principal articles of food, farm implements and machinery and repair parts thereof, rough and dressed lumber, gasoline, illuminating, lubricating and fuel oils, etc., nets, net twines and fishermen's equipment, cements and fertilizers, should be free from customs duties as well as the raw material entering into the same.
These are not my words; they are the words of the Liberal party which has been in office for fourteen years since those promises were placed in their platform and program. I want to see whether I can find out, and the country, I believe, wants to know and ought to be able to know, just how many persons in this house agree with that platform. I say quite frankly that I agree with the proposals contained in that platform. If it is not the policy of the Liberal party, whose government this is, then let the Liberal party cease to divide the people upon an issue which they themselves have largely made an unreal issue in Canada; because wherever you go on the prairies even to-day the speeches of the times to which I have referred still carry weight, still have an effect, and you will find that instead of discussing other economic issues many of our farmers and people on the prairies discuss the merits of the tariff proposals of the Liberal party and consistently vote for that party because they believe that those proposals are a part of the tariff policy of that party.
The hon. gentleman did the same thing to-day.

Well, I do not know that I did. But the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) will have an opportunity of pointing that out a little later.
In other words, if there is a Liberal in this house who believes in his party's official tariff program, I contend he should vote for the subamendment which I have just moved.
Just over two years ago I made the statement in this house that in my judgment the tariff controversy in Canada was largely out of date owing to the fact that such promises as this had not been implemented. And I listened with a good deal of interest to the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) this session stating that in his opinion all we had succeeded in doing in the years that have gone by is to create a great deal of hard feeling and to divide the people. The purpose of my amendment is to test the opinion of the house regarding that policy.

The Budget-Mr. Caldwell

If the Liberal party and the Liberal government of this country will not give an opportunity to the constituents whom I represent in this house to go into the open markets of the world to buy as well as to sell there, then again, using the words of the hon. member for Melville, we must expect some compensating adjustments. If the farmers of the west and other parts of Canada are forced to buy in what is after all a highly protected market, then they have the right to expect that the product which they produce shall be protected, so that they may receive an adequate return for their labour, or in other words, that their products, as in New Zealand, shall receive a proper minimum price which will enable the producers to buy within this protected market in which they have to operate. One or other of these two things it seems to me is a matter of simple justice: either that our producers should be permitted to buy in the open market, if they have to sell there, or that they should be guaranteed their price level, as the manufacturers and other groups are guaranteed a price level by the tariff to-day.
There are many other aspects of the budget which one might discuss. I was of course interested in what the minister had to say regarding the financial outlook of the government. That, however, can be discussed under the Bank of Canada bill which is now before the house, and if I may do so I would here express a great deal of pleasure that the government have seen fit to bring in a bill to nationalize the Bank of Canada.
At last.

At last. The group
with which I am associated has consistently urged this in the house ever since 1921. I should like to see the government go beyond that and exercise greater control over the chartered banks; indeed I should like to see the chartered banks also made public institutions.
The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) made a very interesting comparison in the opening part of his speech. He stated that the average real wage of those employed in 1935 was higher than the average real wage of those employed in 1926. He then went on to show that the earnings of' capital also increased during the same period, but that the returns to the farmers greatly decreased. That statement regarding our farmers of course is quite correct. On the other hand let us bear this in mind, that the hon. member for Huron North was taking all the farmers collectively, but he was in reality, as I understand, taking only

that portion of labour which was employed. Those of us who remember the evidence given before the implements committee, for example, will recollect that the farm implement companies stated that they first dismissed their lower paid and casual employees and endeavoured to retain their permanent employees and officials. Naturally these men received higher wages and salaries, while a number of the other casual employees were forced to go on relief and had no wages. So if you take labour in the mass, I think you will find that it suffered tremendously during the depression. The farmer, of course, and particularly the western farmer, suffered more than anyone else during that period of depression. Capital, however, was represented by substantially the same people who controlled it prior to the depression. There may have been changes here and there; but in the main it was the same group, and it seems to me that in reality that group alone received an increased return during those years of depression. So, if we want to get the picture presented by the hon. member for Huron North clearly in our minds, we must take these factors into consideration.
I do not want to make my speech more lengthy, but I should like to close with the thought with which 1 began. It is this, that the picture presented by the Minister of Finance in the budget clearly indicates that the revenue of this country is largely derived from the great masses of the people. The hon. member for York South spoke of the sales tax and the increase in the revenues from that source since this government took office. There was the enormous sum of $138,000,000 largely taken out of the pockets of the common people of this country by means of that tax. Then there is the sugar tax, which bears heavily on every home in this country. According to these figures, as I have said, the revenue of the country to a very large degree has been derived from the masses of the people.
I should like to see the government consider other ways and means of obtaining necessary revenues. For example, out of our natural resources are extracted huge volumes of wealth by corporations some of which are largely owned by people who do not reside in Canada. At the moment I am thinking of International Nickel, with profits last year in excess of $53,000,000. I am thinking of Consolidated Smelters which last year, out of the resources of this country, made a profit of some $16,000,000 and placed in reserve $3,000,000 to meet profits this year. Then it paid a dividend of $2.50 on the original $5 share. Someone will say that these shares are

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
worth more than $5 to-day. They are not really worth more than S5. That was their original value; but in the open market, by speculation, such shares may be boosted up to $20, $30, $40, $50 or $100.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.
The minister does not agree; nevertheless that is a statement of fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in relation to the companies of which my hon. friend is speaking.

My point is that apart from those considerations enormous profits are being made out of the resources of this country, and the time has come when we ought to look to these resources to provide revenue not for private corporations but for the Dominion of Canada. The present budget is brought down following a year of comparative prosperity; I say "comparative prosperity" for certain groups. There is every evidence of a recession. As the minister intimated, or at least implied, if war industries ceased and the demand for certain Canadian products disappeared, we would find ourselves in a very difficult position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
The minister says he did not imply that. In the course of his speech he stated that our position was not good in every respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, I emphasized that the danger of war, which produced a demand for certain commodities, also reduced the demand for other commodities which depended upon peace and prosperity in the countries which bought our goods. The inference is that if the demand for war materials ceased, then conditions of peace and prosperity would bring about a demand for much more of our other commodities. I am sorry if I did not convey that clearly, because that is what was in my mind in what I had to say.

That was not the impression that I got, and moreover I do not think the minister ought to be so optimistic. I am of the opinion that even if to-morrow the world should reach an agreement regarding disarmament, the tremendous burden of debt created by rearmament would largely nullify the gain that we would make, at least for a considerable time to come. Therefore I say we should be looking to the future and trying to find ways and means of increasing the revenue of the country without adding to the burdens of the common people.
51952-259J

Mr. Speaker, anyone listening to the minister's superb delivery of his budget speech and to the contents of that speech, remembering at the same time that the cry of the suffering is going up throughout the land from coast to coast, could not possibly escape the thought that the minister is a confirmed optimist. He can dress up a gloomy situation to make it look attractive and beautiful better than anyone to whom I have ever listened.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You can do pretty well yourself.

I appreciate the minister's compliment. After having said that I congratulate the minister upon having thus performed, I must say there are some things about the budget which are not quite so attractive. In the first place I believe everyone must grant that this is a rich man's budget. It depends upon taxation and borrowing. Taxation and borrowing -both tend to work in the interests of the rich man and to the disadvantage of the poor. There is, moreover, no new source of money. This both permits and obliges the banking system of Canada to go on creating all of the nation's money. This budget, therefore, is a betrayal of the Canadian people. It betrays the aged, the middle-aged, the youth and the infant in arms. The budget speech either repudiates or qualifies the Liberal party's promises of monetary reform made in 1935 and in previous years.
I turn to page 3902 of this year's Hansard, and I read these words:
There are some, of course, who appear to believe that the government should not pay interest at all or, indeed, should issue debt free money to finance its expenditures or to retire its interest bearing debt or to do both of these things. It is incredible that this hoary fallacy should persist after so many historical demonstrations of its devastating possibilities.
I shall stop for a moment to talk about hoary fallacies. To certain types of mentality everything that has not yet been done is an impossibility. How the minister, with his natural optimism, can.be of that mentality surpasses my understanding to comprehend. Iron was never successfully used for ships and was consequently an impossibility until iron was used for ships. A perusal of the debates in the British House of Commons while they were considering the advisability of introducing iron for the building of ships reminds one strangely of some of the things we hear in this House of Commons when we suggest a change of monetary policy. For example, in the British house one man is reported to have
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

said: "Iron for ships, forsooth! Why not stone for ships, then?"-a question which manifested a great deal of intelligence in that man.
Vaccination for the prevention of disease was apparently an impossibility until it was done. Alchemy, by which one substance was to be changed into another, was for centuries laughed at. It was considered impossible. Ben Jonsen even wrote a play called The Alchemist, in which the credulity of his fellows was laughed off the stage. But, behold! Today we have learned how to change one substance into another. We now have synthetic rayon, rubber, dyes and nitrates. Who knows how much farther we shall go before the wonderful possibilities of this world are exploited? The dream of horseless carriages was a favourite source of amusement to some people, until all of a sudden an age developed in which horseless carriages became a reality.
Merely to look upon our proposals as a hoary fallacy does not reflect altogether to the advantage of the author of those words. We hear quite frequently urged against our contention the question: Has it been tried out? It has never been tried out. National money has never yet been tried out-not even by that king to whom the hon. member referred-in accompaniment with the dividend and the just price. Consequently social credit has never been tried out. And consequently, to certain types of mentality in the house, it is foredoomed to failure, and not worthy of a trial.
May I ask whether or not mine sweepers were a success before they were tried out? Were gas masks a success before they were tried out? If in the defence of London against air attacks they had waited until someone had tried out the devices to be used, I assume London would have been in as bad a position of utterly impotent helplessness as we are to-day in our financial affairs, a position the weakness of which future years will abundantly show.
To proceed with the minister's words:
Perhaps I underestimated the insidious appeal of a program which promises to make something out of nothing, although I must say that for no one more than for a Minister of Finance should such a program have seductive charm.
Perhaps the word " seductive " was wisely chosen, but I doubt it.
Those who are arguing against social credit persist in saying you cannot have something for nothing. Social credit does not propose something for nothing. It never did, and it does not to-day. Not long ago the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) made a remark about something for nothing. In a few

moments I shall comment on the matter; but before going into detail I feel moved to ask hon. members this question: Did any of you ever do anything to repay Shakespeare for writing his plays, or did you get them for nothing? Did you ever do anything in payment for Titian's and Raphael's works? Did you ever do anything in payment for Beethoven's and Mozart's works? People may laugh about this; but after they have thought the matter over long enough they will realize that passed down to this generation have been remarkable inventions, to the enjoyment of which the people of this generation are entitled just as much as we recognize they are entitled to the full enjoyment of the works of Shakespeare, Milton, Raphael and Beethoven. The less any one says in opposition to what I have said, before he has taken time to think, the better off he will be. We will ask anyone if he can devise a means whereby the inventions which have gone into the manufacture of the great machines we have to-day, and which unquestionably, to the extent to which we draw upon our inheritance, belong in some measure to everybody in the community, shall be paid for by those who use and enjoy them in the future. Let us ask anyone and everyone if he can say how we can enable the people to draw dividends from this part of their heritage of the past. I have never mentioned this before, but it is an exceedingly important matter. It is not saying that we want something for nothing; all we are asking for is a right. The minister goes on to say:
How much easier my task would be if I could draw on the accumulated savings of the Canadian people without paying interest thereon

May I point out to the minister that this is a completely erroneous notion of social credit. There is no desire to draw upon the accumulated savings of the people of Canada. It may look impossible to the person who has not studied the theory, but I say now that no one will be worse off. Everyone will be better off. That may seem impossible; nevertheless it is so. Many of these other things which I have mentioned seemed impossible, but they were carried out. The minister continued:
-if indirectly I could do the same thing by issuing credit against our natural wealth, that is, against the resources of farm and forest and mine and factory now owned by the Canadian people as individuals and not by the dominion government.
Here the minister has a right idea of social credit. He says that he cannot draw credit against the resources which are not owned by the dominion government, but let me tell

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
him that for many generations our banking institutions have been doing that very thing to their own profit and to the disadvantage of the people who own those resources.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

That may be questioned now, but I do not think it will be questioned when I have finished. The minister continues:
I am sometimes criticized because I do not accept the so-called "new economics" which is in fact centuries old.
I do not question that it is centuries old, but many of the finest things in this world are centuries old. The minister continues:
It dates back to that monarch-
I shall not read further from the minister's eloquent speech, but I should like to say a word or two about that monarch whom he does not name. He must be left as an uncertainty, an abstraction.
I should like to refer now to the admirable speech made last night by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). In my opinion it was one of the most courageous and effective speeches ever delivered in this house. As the days go on I believe the honour which is due to the hon. member for having delivered that speech under these circumstances will increase. I should like to quote briefly from page 4063 of Hansard:
As a matter of fact, under section 59, subsection 4 of our Bank Act, our chartered banks are now privileged to take a five dollar Bank of Canada bill and to exchange on the security of that five dollars, $100 of bank deposits written into the bank's books by a mere stroke of the pen, for either a one hundred dollar treasury bill or a one hundred dollar interestbearing bond.
While we are talking about getting something for nothing, I should like to direct attention to that achievement of the banks as being a most astonishing example of getting something for nothing. What was it that enabled the country to use those $95 of deposits as money? It was the resoures of the Dominion of Canada which the minister has said you could not draw upon in issuing credit. There may be two notions about the matter, but I believe I could make out an extremely strong case from my standpoint if I had the time, which I have not. The hon. member continues:
That was. the concession which was made to the chartered banks of the government of 1934, and they are not missing the opportunity; for to-day they hold $1,155,000,000 of such securities, an increase of $471,000,000 since that great concession was made when the Bank Act was amended to reduce gold reserves to twenty-five per cent and to reduce cash reserves to five per cent.
And again:

subtopic: SANCTION BY PARLIAMENT OF PLACING OF MILITIA ON ACTIVE SERVICE BEYOND CANADA

speechtext:
Mr. C. G. MacNEIL (Vancouver North) moved the second reading of Bill No. 84, to amend the Militia Act.
He said: This bill has been standing on the order paper for some time. I had hoped that its appearance on the order paper would in itself have been sufficient to direct attention to the necessity of revising an act the language of which is not only antiquated but obsolete in the light of present day circumstances. I would not have proceeded with this bill had I secured any indication that the government contemplated appropriate action in this matter.
In entering upon a discussion of the subject, I am not unmindful of the warning note sounded by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), during the debate on foreign policy, that members of this house should exercise reasonable caution in discussing issues of this kind. Nevertheless, I cannot overlook the fact, to which our attention was directed by the Prime Minister himself, that the trend of international affairs may at any time involve Canada in a very grave crisis. I cannot overlook the fact that in this act we have what are virtually the articles of war for Canada. We have in it the authority under which Canada may mobilize its man power; we have herein the authority under which Canada may participate in an external war. I say I cannot overlook these facts; but I submit that it would be folly verging upon the criminal to face the risks of the impending

crisis without clearly defining and frankly discussing, in relation to our present constitutional status, the authority under which we engage in war.
I wish to make it quite clear at the outset that I am not attempting to discuss or propose changes in commonwealth relations. I am not attempting to discuss or suggest any alteration or change in the status of the crown with regard to dominion affairs. I had before me, in drafting the proposed bill, the Balfour formula of 1926, wherein it is declared that: .	.	. Great Britain and the dominions.	.	. are autonomous communities within
the British empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
I suggest nothing more than that which has already been proposed by the Prime Minister in the assurances he has given to this house and in the speeches he has made at successive imperial conferences, wherein he has said repeatedly that we have no commitments either to maintain neutrality or to engage in a war in the event that the British Empire should be involved in conflict, and that parliament will in the light of the then existing circumstances determine these issues. I have that clearly in mind, and if the bill is examined it will be found that it goes not a step beyond the policy already enunciated by the Prime Minister. I ask simply this, in discussing a matter of purely domestic policy, that there be now written into the statute those assurances which have been given the people of Canada by the Prime Minister; that the language should be clear and explicit with regard to our position in respect of fateful decisions. I ask that we give reality to his statement; that at least we take one step, a step which may easily be taken at this time, to give actual content to some of the assurances made by the Prime Minister.
I may also point out that what I propose is entirely consistent with British practice, and I hope that my friends who adhere to the British-front policy will not suspect me of any attempt to undermine that policy at this time or to suggest separation or secession from the empire. I propose nothing beyond the now recognized status of the dominion within the British Commonwealth of Nations. That which I propose in these bills is entirely consistent with British practice.
May I remind hon. members that the British Army Act, which in 1937 was entitled, "An act to provide, during twelve months for the discipline and regulation of the army and the

Militia Act Amendment
air force", is an act which is re-enacted each year. The parliament at Westminster must meet and must re-enact each year an act providing not only for the establishment of the armed forces of the United Kingdom but also for the discipline of those forces within the United Kingdom and His Majesty's dominions beyond the seas, and it deals in every particular with the control of those forces. Each year that step is taken in addition to the voting of supply for the maintenance of the military, naval and air establishments in Great Britain. I have here excerpts from the Army (Annual) Act of 1937. In the first paragraph of the preamble this is what is found:
Whereas the raising or keeping of a standing army within the United Kingdom in time of peace, unless it be with the consent of parliament, is against law . . .
There is, of course, a definite reason for the British practice in this regard, dating back to the days of the Restoration. In 1803 the statutory articles of war were incorporated in the army act. Those who are students of military law will easily trace back the development of this practice. I am quoting now from the authoritative Manual of Military Law, which states:
The Ai-my Act has of itself no force, but requires to be brought into operation annually by another act of parliament, (generally known as the Army (Annual) Act), thus securing the constitutional principle of the control of parliament over the discipline requisite for the government of the army. These annual acts afford opportunities of amending the Army Act, of which considerable use has been made.
Dealing with this matter, the British people have made it clear for definite reasons that the prerogatives of the crown in this respect shall be limited and shall be subject to the control of parliament. All I ask in this bill and in the companion bill is that we be definitely assured now, by statutory enactment of the control of parliament over three matters: the command of our armed forces, the imposition upon the Canadian people of compulsory military service, and the participation of Canadian forces in external war. You will notice that I recognize the necessity of the executive being completely unhampered and free to make prompt decisions and to act decisively and instantly with regard to emergencies requiring us to repel invasion. I ask that parliament have definite authority to deal with the command of the forces in the first instance, with the imposition of compulsory military service on the Canadian people, and as regards the participation of our forces in overseas war. That is all I ask- definite statutory authority providing for parliamentary control in a manner consonant with the parliamentary control exercized in the United Kingdom over the military forces of that kingdom.
Three questions arise in this regard. The first is, who shall exercise command over the armed forces of the dominion? The act at present reads:
The command in chief of the militia is declared to continue and be vested in the king, and shall be exercised and administered by His Majesty or by the governor general as his representative.
I ask that this be amended in dealing with the exercise of command to include the words "administered by the governor general acting ,by and with the advice of the king's privy council for Canada." I know many will immediately argue that under the Interpretation Act the term "governor general" is held to mean the governor in council. I am well aware that section 23 of the Interpretation Act provides:
When the governor general is authorized to do any act by proclamation, such proclamation is understood to be a proclamation issued under an order of the governor in council; but it shall not be necessary that it be mentioned in the proclamation that it is issued under such order.
But in the definition section of the Interpretation Act we have:
" Governor," " governor of Canada," or "governor general" means the governor general for the time being of Canada, or other chief executive officer or administrator for the time being carrying on the government of Canada on behalf and in the name of the sovereign, by whatever title he is designated.
Section 7 reads:
" Governor in council," or " governor general in council" means the governor general in Canada, or person administering the government of Canada for the time being, acting by and with the advice of, or by and with the advice and consent of, or in conjunction with the king's privy council for Canada.
There would appear to be two distinctly separate functions performed by His Excellency the Governor General. That may seem to be of minor consequence, but I think I should direct to this problem the attention of those who are more familiar with constitutional law than I am. I am at a complete loss to understand our position with regard to this matter, particularly as there is written into the Militia Act a section that makes the Army Act of Great Britain applicable to Canada. In section 69 of the Militia Act it is provided:
The Army Act for the time being in force in Great Britain, the king's regulations, and all other laws applicable to His Majesty's
Militia Act Amendment

troops in Canada and not inconsistent with this act or the regulations made hereunder, shall have force and effect as if they had been enacted by the parliament of Canada for the government of the militia.
I cannot reconcile this section, as drafted in 1904, with our position under the Statute of Westminster wherein it is provided:
No act of parliament of the United Kingdom passed after the commencement of this act shall extend or be deemed to extend to a dominion as part of the law of that dominion unless it is expressly declared in that act that that dominion has requested, and consented to, the enactment thereof.
I cannot find in the Army Act of Great Britain as it stands at the present time any express declaration that the Dominion of Canada has requested or consented to the application of that act to Canada. It is an interesting point that the fact that section 69 still appeara and is in force in Canada is tantamount to a request and consent of the dominion that, in certain respects at least, the Army Act of Great Britain shall now be applicable to the armed forces of this dominion.
In dealing with these three questions which I bring to the attention of the house, it is perhaps well to consider the history of the Militia Act. No one is more familiar with that history than the right hon. gentleman who now holds the portfolio of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). On more than one occasion he has expounded and dealt in detail with the history of the act. At no time did he do so more thoroughly than in June, 1917, when he took issue with the leader of the house at that time in regard to the interpretation of the sections to which I am now directing the attention of the house. The act, as was pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) a few weeks ago, was introduced in 1868, shortly after confederation, by Sir George Cartier, under circumstances vastly different from those which obtain to-day. At that time, dealing with the command or exercise of authority with respect to the armed forces of the dominion, he drafted the section to read:
As provided by the fifteenth section of the British North America Act, 1867, the command-in-chief of the land and naval militia, and of all the naval and military forces of and in Canada, is vested in the queen, and shall be exercised and administered by Her Majesty, personally, or by the governor as her representative.
The act reads:
The militia shall consist of all the male inhabitants of Canada of the age of eighteen years and upward, and under sixty-not exempted or disqualified by law, and being British
[Mr. MacNeil.J
subjects by birth or naturalization; but Her Majesty may require all the male inhabitants of the dominion, capable of bearing arms, to serve in ease of a levee en masse.
Section 5 divides all the male inhabitants of Canada into four distinct classes for the purposes of service. That was compulsory military service. The criticism of the bill, as I read the debates of 1868, was on the ground that the bill destroyed the volunteer system. The Minister of Justice will agree with me, I believe, that Sir George Cartier at that time felt it necessary under the circumstances then existing to impose some form of compulsory military service. As a matter of fact that form was modeled upon the French system then in vogue. The chief opposition to the bill, as one would gather from the debates of that day, was that it destroyed the volunteer system, and I submit that authority of compulsory military service still exists in the present Militia Act, as I shall endeavour to show in the course of my remarks.
Let us consider the circumstances. The war of 1812 was still within the memory of many then living. The government of Canada had suffered and had to deal with disturbances on the border, the St. Alban's raid and the Fenian disturbances, and the Canadian people were, as it was expressed in the debates, fearful of an invasion of combined Russian and American forces. They therefore felt it necessary at that time to have compulsory military service. Sir George Cartier said he hoped to provide forty thousand trained men per annum until ultimately Canada would have an army of trained men numbering seven hundred thousand capable of defending the shores of Canada. It was also stipulated in the act of 1868 that:
Her Majesty may call out the militia or any part thereof for actual service, either within or without the dominion, at any time, whenever it appears advisable so to do by reason of war, invasion or insurrection, or danger of any of them; and the militiamen, when so called out for active service, shall continue to serve for at least one year from the date of their being called out for actual service, if required so to do, or for any longer period which Her Majesty may appoint.
It goes on to provide that, when faced with sudden emergency, her majesty may appoint in command of the Canadian forces an officer of the regular British army. That may have been admirable legislation at the time, and I am merely drawing attention to the reasons which existed for it. In 1883 several acts dealing with the armed forces of the dominion were consolidated. The next important change occurred in 1904, in the

Militia Act Amendment
Militia Act introduced by Sir Frederick Borden. The sections with which the amending bills deal were introduced in their present form-

speechtext:
The act of 1868 was
repealed.

subtopic: SANCTION BY PARLIAMENT OF PLACING OF MILITIA ON ACTIVE SERVICE BEYOND CANADA
speechtext:
Yes. As the leader of the opposition points out, they repealed the acts of 1868 and 1883, and introduced an entirely new bill, and the present sections 64 and 69, as they now stand, were then incorporated in the statute as drafted by Sir Frederick Borden. I think it is important to note the intentions of Sir Frederick Borden with regard to these matters, and on this point I wish to quote the words of the present Minister of Justice speaking on Bill No. 75 in the House of Commons in June, 1917, as reported at page 2520 of Hansard. He said:
Until a few clays ago, I do not think that anybody who has studied the constitutional history of Canada ever expressed the opinion that her militia could be sent overseas by virtue of that act. The debates that took place in 1868 showed that there was no intention to change the principle or the meaning of the section I am discussing. In considering the words "either within or without the dominion" in a subsection we must not forget that Canada at that time included only the four provinces, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and it was important that the authorities should be empowered to send the militia outside of the area of those four provinces to protect and defend the British territory which forms to-day the other provinces of the dominion.
I come now to the Militia Act of 1904.
That is the act to which I am now referring, which is in force to-day.
Surely this act did not change or modify the principles which I have enunciated. The language of the section was made clearer by the insertion of the words "for the defence thereof."
The minister is referring to the section dealing with active service, which now reads:
The governor in council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada and also beyond Canada for the defence thereof at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
The present Minister of Justice continued:
The right hon. Prime Minister quoted a few words from a speech by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, then Minister of Justice. He took good care, it seems to me, not to cite the language of the father of the act, the man responsible for the legislation, and who knows best wrhat was the intention and aim of the bill. Here is the language used by Sir Frederick Borden, then Minister of Militia:
"Mr. Maclean:	I would ask the minister if
it is not the case that under the old section of the law as it now stands the militia of
Canada could be used for the defence of the empire and sent out of this country for that purpose? But under the proposed law that is strictly prohibited.
"Sir Frederick Borden: No. I am advised, and was advised at the time of the South African trouble, for instance, that under the law we could not do that.
"Sir Sam Hughes: Could not do what?
"Sir Frederick Borden:	That we could not
send the militia to South Africa for service; under the law we were not able to do so. The present law has changed, as I say, in conformity with that view, and in sympathy with the idea which, as I said, controls the militia of mother countries and the militia of every one of the colonies of the empire, where you will find precisely the same clause."
On August 1, 1904, in committee, he said:
"Sir Frederick Borden:	. . . The troops we
sent to South Africa were not sent under the militia law at all. They were sent under a special arrangement; they went as volunteers. The same thing could be done at any time. It certainly would not be done under the militia act, either as it was or as we propose to make it, because there is no essential difference. Notwithstanding the fact that my hon. friend from Colchester questions my possession of common sense, I still believe that the act as we propose it is essentially the same in that respect as it was before, the object being to make clear the actual intention."
He said further:
"The very fundamental idea of a militia force always has been, and is now, home defence."
I am sure my hon. friend would not pretend to say that under the law as it is to-day the government could send a corps of the militia upon foreign service.
The Minister of Justice clearly indicated that to be the intention of the men who drafted the present Militia Act.
I wish now to turn for a moment to what actually occurred in 1914. I have the various sessional papers, including the orders in council passed prior to the assembling of parliament on August 18, 1914, and the various dispatches exchanged between His Royal Highness the then Governor General and the British government.
On August 1 this dispatch was sent from the Governor General to the Secretary of State for the Colonies:
My advisers while expressing their most earnest hope that peaceful solution of existing international difficulties may be achieved and their strong desire to cooperate in every possible way for that purpose wish me to convey to His Majesty's government the firm assurance that if unhappily war should ensue the Canadian people will be united in a common resolve to put forth every effort and to make every sacrifice necessary to ensure the integrity and maintain the honour of our empire.
Militia Act Amendment

On August 1 this message was sent from the governor general to the Secretary of State for the Colonies:
In view of the impending danger of war involving the empire my advisers are anxiously considering the most effective means of rendering every possible aid and they will welcome any suggestions and advice which imperial naval and military authorities may deem it expedient to offer. They are Confident that a considerable force would be available for service abroad. A question has been mooted respecting the status of any Canadian force serving abroad as under section 69 of Canadian Militia Act the active militia can only be placed on active service beyond Canada for the defence thereof. It has been suggested that regiments might enlist as imperial troops for stated period, Canadian government undertaking to make all necessary financial provision for their equipment. pay and maintenance. This proposal has not yet been maturely considered here and my advisers would be glad to have views of imperial government thereon.
The Secretary of State for the Colonies to the governor general, August 4, 1914:
Though there seems to be no immediate necessity for any request on our part for an expeditionary force from Canada, I think in view of their generous offer your ministers would be wise to take all legislative and other steps by which they would be enabled without delay to provide such a force in case it should be required later.
From the governor general to the Secretary of State for the Colonies on August 5, 1914:
My government beim; desirous of putting beyond doubt status of Canadian volunteers, request that His Majesty may be pleased to issue an order bringing these volunteers under sections 175 and 176 of the army act.
From the Secretary of State for the Colonies to the governor general, dated August 6, 1914:
With reference to my telegram of August 4. His Majesty's government gratefully accept offer of your ministers to send expeditionary force to this country and would be glad if it could be despatched as soon as possible. Suggested composition follows.
Again on August 8 from the Secretary of State for the Colonies to the governor general:
Referring to my telegram sixth August army council state that a certain proportion of army troops will be required in addition to force mentioned. You will be furnished later on with suggested numbers.
I might go on and read numerous other messages. I refer to order in council P.C. 2067 dated August 6, 1914, which I think is important for the purpose of this discussion:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated August 6, 1914, from the Minister of Militia and Defence, representing, in view of the state of war now existing between the United Kingdom, and the dominions, colonies and dependencies of the British Empire on the one side, and Germany

on the other side, creating a menace to the wellbeing and integrity of the empire, and having regard to the duty of the Dominion of Canada as one of those dominions to provide for its own defence and to assist in maintaining the integrity and honour of the empire, that it is desirable to mobilize militia units of the various arms of the service of such effective strength as may from time to time be determined by Your Royal Highness in Council, such units to be composed of officers and men who are willing to volunteer for overseas service under the British crown; to organize and equip them for war and to make and perfect all arrangements necessary to enable them to enlist and be enrolled for service under His Majesty's Government, should that government so desire.
The minister recommends, in order that this purpose may be carried out, that Your Royal Highness authorize the raising and equipment of such units of such effective strength as aforesaid, the concentrating of them at some point to be selected by the Minister of Militia, with Your Royal Highness's approval, and to make and perfect all arrangements necessary to enable them to enlist and be enrolled for service under His Majesty's government should that government so desire, upon such terms of engagement and for such service as may be deemed advisable.
I could go on and read the various documents on record, but I think I have read enough to show that on every essential point Canada was committed, prior to the assembling of parliament, to participation in external war. I could read the War Measures Act introduced in the house on August 19, 1914, which merely gave blanket ratification to those steps which committed Canada irrevocably at that time to participation in overseas war without the consent of parliament. That was determined under the authority of the statute which I now desire to amend. That statute is still in force. The historic precedent exists. Canada was committed to war without the consent of parliament, and that authority may again be invoked without the consent of parliament. I wish to make it clear that I am not criticising the action of those men who faced terrific responsibility under the most trying circumstances in 1914; I merely point to the facts as they exist. Surely we may profit to some degree from that experience, and if the assurance of the Prime Minister that parliament will now decide, under the constitutional status which we have attained, by reason very largely of Canada's sacrifices in the great war, means anything at this time, surely there can be no objection to the amendments which I propose to the Militia Act. If there is any failure to amend that act, the suspicion must lie in the minds of many that it is the intention again to invoke its authority in the same manner as in 1914.

5.	It is hereby declared that war has continuously existed since the fourth day of August, 1914, and shall be deemed to exist until the governor in council by proclamation published in The Gazette declares that it no longer exists-
Now I wish to turn to the situation which arose in respect to the Military Service Act of 1917. In the preamble of that act the sections to which I referred are definitely quoted as indicating the necessity for the Military Service Act. Section 41 and section 69 of the Militia Act are quoted, and the justification for the Military Service Act, as the Minister of Justice will remember quite clearly, was that such authority had existed previously in the Militia Act. It was argued by the late Sir Robert Borden, by his Minister of Justice and by various supporters of the government at that time that from 1914 to 1917 authority had existed and could have been invoked under the Militia Act not only for the dispatch of an overseas expeditionary force but, if they had so desired, for the imposition of compulsory military service on the people of Canada; and, as I say, the justification for the Military Service Act of 1917 was that it was more desirable to have the method of selective draft rather than the system of balloting which is now in the act; for I contend that the compulsory military service feature is still contained in this act. As I stated a moment ago, all male inhabitants of Canada are still liable for military service and may be summoned to the colours by order of the governor general in case of a levee en masse; and for the purpose of enrolment even in peace time the male inhabitants of Canada at present are divided into four classes and may be required to serve for a stated period. Of course that is obsolete in practice; but it is still in the act and that authority may be invoked if it should be so desired. I am not suggesting for a moment

that the right hon. Prime Minister has the faintest desire to do so; but the language of the statute is obsolete in the light of the assurance of the Prime Minister and the present constitutional status of the dominion.
May I also point out that in the debate to which I refer it was quite apparent that there was a wide divergence of opinion, and I commend the debates of 1914 as well as those of June, 1917, to all members of this house for careful study at this time. As I say, the Prime Minister of the day, Sir Robert Borden; his Minister of Justice, and many other eloquent and able gentlemen argued that the authority existed in the Militia Act. They quoted the opinion of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick who, in dealing with the interpretation of these sections, particularly section 69, said:
The governor in council may send the militia of Canada out of Canada at any time when deemed necessary for the defence of Canada. If, in the opinion of the governor general in council it should be necessary, because of a war going on in India, to send militia out there for the defence of Canada, they may, in the exercise of their discretion, do it, because they are the sole judges of what is necessary to be done in the defence of Canada.
Then he went on to say:
But we do not think it advisable that that power should be absolutely and unrestrictedly in the hands of the governor in council. We think it advisable that the period during which they may exercise that powder should be restricted and that parliament should be called together and be consulted at the earliest opportunity. Parliament must be summoned in fifteen days and then the whole matter will be in the hands of the people's representatives.

subtopic: SANCTION BY PARLIAMENT OF PLACING OF MILITIA ON ACTIVE SERVICE BEYOND CANADA
speechtext:
I am pointing out that the leaders of the political parties at that time-and I am not saying whether they were right or wrong, nor am I trying to revive discussion of the conscription issue-were divided in their opinions on this question. There were differences between able constitutional lawyers at that time, who were faced with tremendous responsibilities. Sir Wilfrid Laurier took direct issue, as he said, with the opinion of Sir (Robert Borden on this very matter. The government of the day acted on the interpretation given by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, a former Minister of Justice and later Chief Justice of Canada. The sections of the Militia Act now under discussion are quoted in the preamble of the Military Service Act. I mention this incident to show that serious ambiguity exists, and I fail to understand why the Minister of Justice, having found himself in that position in 1917, has failed to amend the act as it stands to-day, so as to make the position clear that parliament has definite control over decisions as to compulsory military service and as to dispatch of troops beyond the frontiers of Canada.
Let me refer to one other point. Speaking of the advisability of frankness in discussion prior to the event, in May, 1918, there was serious disaffection in Canada, and that disaffection was brought to a head by the descent upon Ottawa of a delegation of four thousand farmers. They submitted through the present hon. member for Outre-mont (Mr. Vien), who was in the house at that time, a most remarkable document, from which I wish to quote briefly. It indicates the results which follow arbitrary executive action without reference to parliament, and the results which follow a failure to bring these matters under frank discussion. At page 2551 a remarkable document was read into
Hansard as submitted by representatives of the agricultural community. I quote in part:
Will the house permit us to speak more plainly what is in our minds? We have never believed that the conditions produced by the war demanded flagrant departures from the honoured processes of law enjoined by the constitution while parliament is in session or is near assembling. We believe that reliance upon parliament, instead of upon arbitrary authority, most effectively honours the guarantees of freedom which are embedded in the constitution. One considerable departure from sound practice may be accepted, but repetitions of it may be exceedingly dangerous, especially under such circumstances as now beset the state.
Twelve days before the meeting of parliament in January, 1916, the authorized Canadian army was doubled from 250,000 to 500,000 men. No British army had ever been doubled without recourse to parliament. That it was done in Canada caused students of British history to inquire whether anything had occurred to warrant such a disregard of parliament. Though this House of Commons has inherited some of the consequences of such an innovation, we desire to confine our respectful remonstrances to more recent events.
It goes on to speak of riots in Quebec, unhappy circumstances through the agricultural communities, and the effect of the order in council endorsed by parliament which virtually swept aside the provisions of the Military Service Act of 1917. In view of the history of the Militia Act, the setting in which it was originally drafted, and in view of its inadequacy between 1914 and 1918, and the doubt which existed as to its exact interpretation, and as to the authority of the executive with regard to decisions of vital consequence, surely I am within my rights in urging the government to accept the amendments I have proposed.
It is intelligent and wise to act prior to the event. I say it is better far to face these decisions to-night, even though there may be sharp disagreement on some matters, than in face of grave emergency to have strife and dissension and disputes, such as I have referred to to-night in the quotations I have brought to the attention of the house. I say the Prime Minister might very well accept the amendment and keep faith with the youth of Canada whose lives are at stake, and who may be commandeered by the executive without reference to parliament under the terms of the Militia Act as it stands on the statute books of Canada to-day.

subtopic: SANCTION BY PARLIAMENT OF PLACING OF MILITIA ON ACTIVE SERVICE BEYOND CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the measure with some hesitation, because it does indeed involve a highly technical constitutional question and one which perhaps might better be left to the consideration of legal authorities.
Militia Act Amendment

Nevertheless I have long felt that our position concerning this particular matter has never been clear and explicit enough, and it is my view that the measure now before the house would make the act clear and explicit beyond the shadow of a doubt.
I also keep in mind the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he told us to be very careful about what we had to say concerning foreign policies. Nevertheless I believe that because of the existing situation certain principles should always be kept in mind, and in that connection I am reminded of the expressions of Sir Edward Grey, otherwise known as Viscount Grey of Fallodon, a former Secretary of the Foreign office during at least part of the great war. Referring to the situation at that time he said:
Every country had been piling up armaments and perfecting preparations for war. The object in each case had been security. The effect had been precisely the contrary of what was intended and desired. Instead of a sense of security there had been produced a sense of fear, which was yearly increasing. Europe was afraid of the German army. Germans encouraged in themselves and in others the belief that the German army was invincible.
I pause to point out that he was referring to conditions then existing. Perhaps the situation to-day is not similar. But the conclusion which he drew from his thoughts at that time are just as true to-day as they were then.
Such was the general condition of Europe; preparations for war had produced fear, and fear predisposes to violence and catastrophe.
So, keeping that principle in mind, I feel it is simply supporting the stand taken by the Prime Minister that our position should be made clear in respect to our attitude concerning this particular question. For example, it was for that reason that on March 16, 1938, I tried to introduce a bill which would have had the effect of repealing the Military Service Act of 1917. Hon. members will recall the discussion which took place at that time when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) assured us that the act was dead. As a matter of fact he said it was a "dead horse", and other similar references were made to the act at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SANCTION BY PARLIAMENT OF PLACING OF MILITIA ON ACTIVE SERVICE BEYOND CANADA
speechtext: And that was true.

subtopic: SANCTION BY PARLIAMENT OF PLACING OF MILITIA ON ACTIVE SERVICE BEYOND CANADA
speechtext:
The purpose I had in trying to introduce the bill was to attempt to make our position in Canada as clear and explicit as we possibly could. No one can deny that since we are a part of the British Empire we must face our responsibilities in that connection. It is true the Prime Minister has assured us on many occasions that the people of Canada would be consulted, through 
parliament, if any action of that kind were taken. Yet when we notice the events taking place around us to-day we cannot help pointing with wonder at the words of Sir Thomas Inskip, Coordination of Defence Minister, who spoke in the British parliament just before midnight on May 31 of this year. The press report is as follows:
James Ede, Labour, said last night that from Sir Thomas' statement it was clear the government had "legislative machinery" for conscription ready to be used as soon as war should break out.
"I have said so as plainly as I could," the minister replied.
He went on to say:
With the experience of 1914, the government departments concerned have given a great deal of consideration over a number of years to the best use of man power in an emergency.
There is certain to be, in the event of war, a competent authority who will allocate, according to the age and capacity of each individual person, a suitable position for that person to occupy.
But nobody would escape from the obligation which would be placed upon him in those circumstances by choosing a position, possibly one which he might think more attractive for himself, in peace time.
If anybody elects to join one or the other of the many services asking for recruits at the present time, he will do so with full realization that he will not thereby be exempt from any obligation which parliament may impose upon him in time of war.
That is the declaration of Sir Thomas Inskip in the British parliament. I feel it was said simply because the present world situation, although it has quieted somewhat within recent weeks, is felt to be serious in Great Britain, and certain measures are being taken so that all things might be in readiness in the event of an outbreak of war.
Because of what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, I feel that every member of this house should support this measure, particularly the hon. members from the province of Quebec and elsewhere who have always felt they should be consulted before any such action was taken by the parliament of Canada. I should like to quote from the speech of the Prime Minister as follows:
"What I have said and quoted-"
I am still quoting what I said at Geneva two years ago.
"-does not mean that in no circumstances would the Canadian people be prepared to share in an action against an aggressor; there have been no absolute commitments either for or against participation in war or other forms of force. It does mean that any decision on the part of Canada to participate in war will have to be taken by the parliament or people of Canada in the light of all existing circumstances; circumstances of the day as they exist in Canada, as well as in the areas involved."

Militia Act Amendment
In order to bring about that happy condition, I consider that the present Militia Act should be amended. Section 4 of the Militia Act reads:
The command in chief of the militia is declared to continue and be vested in the king, and shall be exercised and administered by His Majesty or by the governor general as his representative.
It does not say the governor general in council, nor does it refer in any other way to the parliament of Canada. There may be other limitations, but that is the language of that particular statute. In order to determine our exact position, we should know what are the powers of the governor general and who is the governor general of Canada. I hold in my hand the statutes of Canada, 1930, second session, and I should like to read from the prefix thereof relating to the letters patent constituting the office of the governor general of Canada. This reads:
Letters patent under the great seal of the realm, constituting the office of Governor General and Commander in Chief of the Dominion of Canada. Dated 23rd, March, 1931.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend read section 15 of the British North America Act in conjunction with that?

subtopic: SANCTION BY PARLIAMENT OF PLACING OF MILITIA ON ACTIVE SERVICE BEYOND CANADA
speechtext:
I am coming to that. I just wanted to make it clear how the governor general was appointed, and in a few minutes I shall refer to the powers of the governor general as set out in the British North America Act. I quote:
Office of Governor General and Commander in Chief constituted.
We do hereby constitute, order, and declare that there shall be a Governor General and Commander in Chief in and over our Dominion of Canada (hereinafter called our said dominion), and appointments to the said office shall be made by commission under our sign manual and signet.
I wanted this to be placed upon the record during the course of my remarks to show definitely how the appointment of the governor general is made. Section 15 of the British North America Act reads:
The command in chief of the land and naval militia, and of all naval and military forces, of and in Canada, is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the queen.
It does not state that it is vested in the governor general in council. Executive power is outlined under sections 9 and 10 of the British North America Act, which read:
9.	The executive government and authority of and over Canada is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the queen.
10.	The provisions of this act referring to the governor general extend and apply to the governor general for the time being of Canada,
or other the chief executive officer or administrator for the time being carrying on the government of Canada on behalf and in the name of the queen, by whatever title he is designated.
There is some reason for those of us who are not well versed in legal matters to believe that there may be room for disagreement in connection with the status of Canadians at the present time. In my opinion the present bill will serve to a large degree to clear up the situation. It will also serve to bring into effect the declarations made by the right hon. Prime Minister, that the people of Canada should be consulted in case of war. I could go on and refer to the fear which is in the hearts of so many people at the present time as to the outbreak of war. We realize the serious situation which exists in Europe, and we fear that our ties with other countries may involve us in war. I am not at the moment discussing our relationship to the British Empire or to Great Britain, but I do believe that as a part of the British Empire we must of necessity assume the responsibilities which exist at the present time and which must be faced. The words to be added by this bill to section 4 of the act are:
-acting by and with the advice of the king's privy council for Canada.
The other amendments proposed by the bill are along the same lines.
I intend to support this bill, and I want to make my position quite clear. I well remember during the election campaign of 1935 when I was asked many times to state my position in connection with war. In every instance I always replied I believed that in ease Canada was invaded, every Canadian should be willing to give to the very last of anything that he possessed, even his life, in order to defend the country that he loved and the family that he had raised, but before he was sent overseas to take part in any war beyond the borders of Canada he should be entitled to express his opinion as to whether or not the reasons for that war were such that he could support. I do not wish to discuss the propaganda which is usually carried on at such time and which has such an influence upon public opinion. The fundamental principle of democracy which is involved is not altered in any degree. The individual who may be called upon to give up his life elsewhere should have the right to say whether he is willing to do so. I believe everyone in Canada desires to have that great privilege.
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
