subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with the remainder of the contribution which I am endeavouring to make to the budget debate, I should like to say, in criticism of the budget, that as a westerner and a representative of an agricultural constituency I protest against the fact that no effort has been made to reduce the duties on and the prices of, farm machinery to the farmers, and that no provision has been made for the reduction of the sales tax. Both of these matters bear heavily upon the people in my constituency and throughout the west.
When the house took recess at six o'clock I was referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Mc-Geer) as reported on page 4067 of Hansard, to the effect that he did not approve social credit principles. From what the hon. member said with reference to the issuing of purchasing power, one is forced to the conclusion that there is not much difference between his idea as to where the money could come from and the idea of those who believe in the social credit movement. Inasmuch as the origin of new money is the first all-important matter rather than what you shall do with the money after you get it, I contend that he was hardly justified in making so sweeping a statement as is to be found in column two of the page to which I referred. However, his opinions are his; ours are ours; and he has a perfect right to say what he likes. There is apparently this difference between his idea concerning money and ours. He did not, so far as I was able to understand, lay down in his speech the principle that the new money should not cause debt. Our stand is that when new money is created there should not be any debt of the government for that money; if anyone owes anybody for that money, he should owe the government of the country for the money. To us it is an absurdity that the government of a country should owe anybody in the country for the money that government has with which to carry on, or for the money which is created

within the country. It is the unchallengeable, sacred, sovereign right of the government of the country to create such money as it is necessary to create within the country.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard did not say anything about the just price. I think he would be in a difficult position in maintaining an objection to the just price. It has not been discussed to any great extent, but certainly a just price commends itself to any fair-minded person.
As to what shall be done with respect to the dividend, may I raise just one or two questions for the benefit of the hon. member and other hon. members in this chamber? He mentioned last night the great amount of money which the British government was expending to increase purchasing power by an impressive rearmament program. He mentioned rehousing and a great many other projects which are being carried on to distribute purchasing power among the people. Let me ask this question first: When the rearmament program ceases, how will the government proceed to get the money into circulation? That question must be answered. And when rehousing has gone forward to as great a degree as is considered advisable under the conditions, how will an amount of money similar to that which has been expended through rehousing be distributed among the people? The same question might be asked with respect to each of the projects proposed. Again, it must be borne in mind that when any project is set forth and effected within a country, there are but a limited number of the people of that country who are enabled to get employment in connection with that project. The result is that a great many people to whom the purchasing power should come are unable by any ordinary means to get that purchasing power into their hands. The all-important matter is to get the purchasing power into the hands of the consumers. The hon. member will be faced with the difficulty of getting around that objection unless he accepts the principle of the dividend.
Let me turn for a brief time to the question of money. The Minister of Finance, whether he intended to or not, gave the impression that attempts in the past to use money by a government have been failures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In this connection let me refer hon. members to an extremely fine book, published in 1930, called The Theory and Principles of Central Banking, by Doctor William A. Shaw, editor of the calendar of treasury records of His Majesty's public

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
records office. He is the author of seven successful books on monetary topics. There can 'be very little doubt that this man is one of the world's most eminent authorities. On page 50 of that book, which is to be found in the library, appear these words:
And thereupon the treasury offered to sell them currency notes at full face price without limit, and at the same time opened a currency note redemption fund for the purpose of retiring the issue as soon as the need for it was over.
What is being discussed here is the means which the British government used to overcome the financial crisis with the banks,, which crisis arose when the war broke out and they had a panic. I go on with the quotation:
To the treasury's surprise, the currency note quickly struck root, and proved itself completely acceptable, and gradually the treasury realized that the whole circulation of the country could be changed over to paper and the gold withdrawn. The changeover was accomplished with astonishing ease and speed by 1916. By the restrictions which were later placed on the movement of gold this currency note circulation became virtually inconvertible, though it was not declared so by law until 1925.
Thus far there seems to have been little difficulty in making this national currency work. I turn again to page 51 and read the following words:
To this currency note circulation there was at first no limit fixed. It could fall or rise unhampered, according to the community's demand or need of it, and in the remaining years of the war and of the armistice period it bore the strain of increased prices and enormously increased production without friction or effort. For the first time in history the world had a sample of a truly automatic currency, issued only by the state, sold only at full face value, supplied or retired in complete accordance and response to the community's unfettered demand or need.
May I stop just for a minute to comment. It is one of the fundamental ideas of the social credit proposals that the money in circulation shall depend upon the needs of the people; in other words, that we should have economic democracy to the fullest degree. Consequently this monetary experience has a most important bearing upon the social credit contention. To continue the quotation:
After ten years of illuminating experience this perfect, uncontrolled, and uncontrollable automatic currency system was thrown over, the automatic principle was surrendered, and our currency, although declared by law to be inconvertible paper, was placed (or was supposed to be placed) under the control of the Bank of England, and became once again sensitive (or was supposed to be made sensitive) to the vagaries of a fluctuating gold cover fund.
The indications from the words used there are that if that change had not been made, this inconvertible paper currency, issued by the state and by the state only, would have been a most outstanding success. On page 57 we read further:
The historical survey agrees with pure theory in declaring that currency control is not and cannot be a function of a central bank, and that paper currency must be entirely automatic alike in its issue and its retirement, just as the previous metallic gold circulation had been, and therefore that the control of it lies in the community, not in the central bank.
May I point out, pausing for a moment, that the idea is economic democracy; that the community itself shall decide (the amount of money which shall be in circulation. To continue the quotation:
In this perfect form such paper is incapable of overissue and debasement, and is therefore proof against manipulation at the hands of a needy government. Therefore the guarantee which Europe is seeking against inflationism resides not in a central bank (which is no guarantee at all), but in an automatic currency.
Such is the verdict which I deduce from this rapid survey of European banking and currency history of the last hundred years.
In the light of such expressions as that, in a book written by so eminent an authority, any man inside this house or out who undertakes to point the finger of scorn at the economic reformer, the advocate of money reform, is being reckless in an extremely high degree.
May I now deal for a few minutes with what has actually happened with respect to the growth of money in another country; I refer to the United States. The information which I am now going to put on Hansard is drawn from pages 66 to 68 of a book called Inflation, by Woodward and Rose, published in 1933. In those two pages will be found the following illuminating figures:

Until 1860 there was very little difference between the amounts of coin and currency and bank deposits, but notice the tremendous jump in the use of bank deposits-figures in a book -iin these later years. In 1930 the coin and currency was $29.76 per capita; bank deposits, $485.57 per capita, and the total circulation medium $515.33 per

capita. The figures which are given on these two pages show the way in which bank deposits, created by the banks out of nothing, constituting nothing but figures in a book, came rapidly to be the money which was used by the country. The figures are extremely striking. The last figures I gave indicate that in the United States in 1930 there was only $29.76 of coin and bills, what we ordinarily call money, while there was 1485.57 of bank deposits. There is a common fallacious notion among people that bank deposits are in some way coin and currency, but these figures show clearly that such is not the case; for as I have just said, and I repeat, in 1930 there was only $29.76 of coin and currency per capita in the United States, while bank deposits amounted to $485.57 per capita-[DOT] figures in a book.
The question is, who created these deposits? The banks of the United States, working through a hundred years of time; and our contention is simply that the government should have created that money. The government and not the banks should have owned it.
Let me turn now to another quotation. These quotations may be rather uninteresting, but they are the best means I can find of convincing anyone who is open-minded and willing to .be convinced. So far as the others are concerned, there is no use in bothering with them.
On page 181 of a book called Controlling Depressions, by Paul Douglas, professor of economics of Chicago university in 1935, we find these words:
Finally, it may be asked why private interests should be allowed to obtain the wealth which comes from the creation of monetary purchasing power in the form of bank credit. As Carl Snyder has shown, production, if we take long periods of time, has increased at a rate of approximately three per cent a year compounded. Now if the private bankers only increase the quantity of credit in the same proportion they would gather to themselves a very large gain in wealth and power.
There, may I point out, is something for nothing, something that has been acquired by the bankers of the United States through all the history of banking in that country.
This has most certainly been the ease in the ast. The volume of bank credit which has een built up from very small beginnings is now the property of the banking fraternity. By creating credit they have acquired a title to wealth and a claim upon the national income as real as if they had themselves built gigantic factories, railroads, utility plants, etc. Some idea of how much these sums amount to can be gained from the fact that if we were to take a credit total of thirty-three billion as our base, an increase of three per cent in this figure to match the secular increase in production would mean that in the very first year the

private bankers would create one billion dollars in new credit. They would own this and would in fact increase their wealth by that much. Ab the total volume of credit rose, the absolute yearly additions would of course rise also. Thus, three per cent of fifty billion would amount to 1-5 billion a year. A large part of the fruits of progress, therefore, tend to be transferred to the private bankers because their ability to create the monetary counters enables them to claim title to the goods. It is, of course, true that this purchasing power is then loaned out. But interest is charged for the loans and these go not only to independent business men but also frequently, as the revelations of the last ten years have shown, to persons and syndicates closely identified with or controlled by the bankers themselves.
There are other quotations from this book which I shall read. Although they are not interesting to listen to, they make interesting reading. On page 182 the author says:
The bankers as individuals are not, of course, to be blamed for this creation of purchasing power. Under the prevailing rules of the game they have been given this power and they have acted both within their legal and their moral rights. But the question remains whether the rules themselves are best for society.
Social credit says that the rules are not best for society; that they should be changed, and that it is the responsibility of this government at this time to change the rules:
Society has long since taken away from individuals the right to profit individually by privately coining money. Why should it surrender to private individuals and corporations the similar right to levy toll upon the public by permitting them to create purchasing power in the form of credit? Should not the profits of this essentially public function accrue to society as a whole rather than to those who have placed themselves at the vantage points of industry?
These are the words of Professor Paul H. Douglas, professor of economics of the university of Chicago. They sound like social credit, but here is an orthodox economist of the United States writing in this vein. In the light of the fact that so eminent a man makes such a contention, reckless indeed is he who has offensive things to say about monetary reformers. On the same page he writes:
There has always been a considerable volume of opinion in favour of the complete nationalization of banking. In the past, its advocates have been regarded as money cranks hovering on the lunatic fringe of social reform. The sentiment in favour of such a policy has, however, been swelling rapidly in both Great Britain and the United States during this depression. In Great Britain, the Labour party has been putting such a proposal near the head of its program, and while no such strong political forces have as yet advanced similar demands in this country such developments do not seem as impossible in the future as they once did. The most cogent argument in favour of such complete nationalization

The Budget-Mr. Harris
which has been advanced in this country is that of Doctor John Bauer and Nathaniel Gold in their recent book, Permanent Prosperity and How to Obtain It.
There are other passages that follow immediately which any hon. member would find interesting. The finding of this outstanding author is that the government and the people should have the profit that comes from the creation of money.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
After listening to social
credit, something about which most of us do not seem to know a great deal, perhaps hon. members will now listen to something about which they know or ought to know a great deal.
Canada is faced to-day with problems of great magnitude. First and foremost among them I place the fact that close to one million of her men, women and children find themselves leaning on the state for daily sustenance. The cost this year will be about
868,000,000. Another problem which is costing us a great deal of money is our railway problem; even as it was last year, the cost will be close to $42,000,000, if not more than that. We have an agricultural problem that is and will be with us for many years to come; young men and young women as they come to maturity find themselves drifting from the farm to the town. Sixty years ago twenty-two people were in the towns to seventy-eight on the farms. To-day in Ontario we find thirty-nine on the farm producing for the wants of sixty-one in the urban centres. Coming to the urban centres, we find one of the greatest problems is that of real estate taxation, which makes it difficult for our people, who are home loving people and like to own their own homes, to do so. These problems are the concern 51952-260J
not only of members of this house but particularly of the ministers, and we should have some action from them. The greatest of all problems is the fact that so many of our people cannot find a vocation. True, the matter of sales tax was dealt with, a nonwork-producing tax, and some degree of relief has been given. Still I say the greatest problem is that of our fellow citizens who cannot find a vocation.
The budget itself quite properly was divided into its five classifications; financial operations, trade, the balance sheet, the estimate of revenue and expenditure, and ways and means to meet that expenditure. But why was not equal weight given to each of these five divisions? Why was one hour spent on trade, one on accounts, information with regard to which we can get each and every month from the blue-books, and only half a page devoted to the forecast for the coming year and half a page on ways and means to meet that cost? Why was nothing of any consequence said- only 217 words-with regard to the railway problem which is exercising the minds of all Canada? To my mind this presentation, to put it as kindly as I can, is one of the greatest examples of inaction that I have seen during my term of sixteen years in this House of Commons. "Vote Liberal and get action." What empty words! Trade and Commerce took one hour. I think the time has come when perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) might take charge of that portion, elaborate the picture for us, and sit in this house and answer, relieving the Minister of Finance of that part of the burden. But inasmuch as the Minister of Finance takes it on himself to talk to us for an hour on trade and commerce, perhaps I may be spared a few minutes.
Trade. Your Liberal god seems to be total trade. You think only in terms of total trade. There I draw the line of demarcation between the Liberal party and the Conservative party. You worship at the shrine of total trade; with us, trade, yes, trade wherever we can get it, expanding trade, but trade of a kind that will not take away from our citizens their handicrafts, their vocations. That is the kind of trade for which we stand. The Liberal party look to the south for more trade, and there they find people much the same as our people, their vocations the same as ours, their mode of living the same, their resources very much the same, the same kind of products and much the same geographical position. What is the result when you give concessions to a powerful nation like that? Each concession you give turns out in the
The Budget-Mr. Harris

long run to be detrimental to the best interests of our country. The action taken by them, particularly during the last two or three decades, we all know has resulted in stifling us and barring us from making real progress. The United States to my mind should receive a secondary consideration in regard to our trade. You have the spectacle of us sitting here for five months waiting for that nation to make up its mind whether or not it is going to enter into a trade agreement with us. That is another example of leaning on that country and not going ahead and functioning as a government, and presenting the budget in March, as it ought to have been presented. Let us go ahead and do the business of Canada, instead of sitting back and waiting five months for the powerful nation to the south of us to make up its mind what it is going to do. Let us carry on and show a stiff front to the rest of civilization, not letting ourselves remain in the category of an adjunct to the United States.
Then, following the same line of thought that total trade is the god, we have in the budget address a table, appearing on page 3896 of Hansard, setting out the imports from the United States, $393,000,000 in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1937, and exports to the United States, of $364,000,000 in the same year. They add the two together and say that is the total trade. But the total trade is not the real factor which affects the economy of this country; it is the balance of trade. Those figures should have been deducted, exports from imports, to show our unfavourable balance with the United States. In 1938 we see the total imports rising to $487,000,000 and exports shrinking by some $21,000,000. But they are added together and the total set before the people of Canada
as an increase of $72,000,000. Had our exports to the United States been deducted from our imports from that country, it would have shown an unfavourable balance of $144,000,000. That is the factor which is seriously affecting our economy. That is the factor which should receive the attention of every sound thinking Canadian. That $144,000,000 unfavourable trade balance represents goods half of which could have been produced or made in Canada. Why give away $2,000,000 a week of Canada's home market, the products of our farms, gardens, orchards and factories? Why give away $1,000,000 a week in wages to purchase the products of United States farms and gardens and factories? I almost heard a tremble in the minister's voice when he handed out that little sop to the west by saying that during his term of office the free imports into this country have increased from one-third to one-half. So much was I interested that I looked to see what classes of goods these imports were. I found an increase in agricultural and vegetable products of a kind that we could produce in this country of $8,000,000 from 1936 to 1937. Analysing that figure I found that in the same year fresh vegetable imports of a kind that we can produce here increased from $4,180,000 to $5,140,000, or twenty-five per cent in one short year. Seeing that, I thought to myself again that the time has come when a party will have to be put in power whose goal is not only more trade, but trade of a kind which will not affect the natural production of our dominion.
With the permission of the house I should like to put the following tabulation on the record. The budget shows the trade of Canada with the United States on page 3896 of Hansard:

The Budget-Mr. Harris
In connection with mixed farming in Canada, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, when I noticed from the statistics that twelve million tons of canned beef came into this country last year, knowing that this represents thirty thousand cattle, I thought once more that the time had come when we should call a halt to importations of that kind. Can we not produce beef in Canada?
Turning to the other side of our national life, industry, and looking at the iron and steel industry, we find that imports increased from $114,000,000 in 1936 to $150,000,000 in 1937; yet in the report of the national employment commission it is stated that there were 99,157 men engaged in that trade in
1929, of whom 35,000 were walking the streets in 1936. Why, then, should we import an additional $40,000,000 worth of iron and its products, while so many of our own people found themselves on the streets looking for jobs? Take the schedule of all commodities entering Canada and divide it up, as the bureau of statistics does, into raw materials, semi-manufactured articles and fully manufactured articles, and what do we find has happened in the last four years? Our total imports have increased from $238,000,000 to $487,000,000, an increase of $249,000,000, or more than double.
I put this record on Hansard:

The fully manufactured products, in every $100 of which there is contained $40 of workmanship and wages, showed an increase from $133,414,768 to $317,851,663, or a total increase of $184,436,895. Yet in his budget speech the Minister of Finance says that "Canada cannot give to-day and trade to-morrow." Within the last three or four years Canada has given more than $184,000,000 in this way alone; yet she wants to trade to-morrow. I say we ought to adhere to the policy that Canada cannot give to-day; and I am behind the minister in that policy. I would even follow him if he went one step further and said Canada should protect the opportunity for workmen in this country to fabricate the goods we need, even beyond the point of giving and even to the extent of protecting ourselves. The Conservative policy that brought about "our" great empire trade agreements-and I said "our" empire trade agreements-did that very thing; saw to it first that the products of our own artisans and farmers were protected against the inroads of materials of all kinds from other countries, and then we had something with which to make a deal; we had some opportunity to bargain.
Canada has been in this position on other occasions; we have been brought to this situation many times through the advent of Liberal governments, and each time they come
to power it seems that more and more of the products of other countries come to our land, while we produce less and less of our own requirements. That happened in the seventies, and the situation was remedied by the national policy of the Conservative party. It happened again in 1890 and 1900, and then in 1911 Canada said, in no uncertain voice, "No more of that." It happened again after the depression of 1930. I say to the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) who seems to have forgotten that there was a depression, that it was not only the depression which was responsible for the extent to which Canada's economic position was affected in 1930. The tremendous importations into this country of goods of a kind that we could produce was also responsible for the difficulty in which we found ourselves. In spite of the fact that "do nothing to aggravate or provoke the United States" seems to be the attitude of our friends opposite, I say that what happened in days gone by is happening again to-day; and if we continue to slip as we have this year, to the extent of an unfavourable trade balance of $100,000,000, it will not be long before something will have to be done. If it is not done, the people of Canada again will call in the Conservative party to straighten matters out.
The Budget-Mr. Harris

This weak, spineless attitude of not aggravating or provoking a nation so powerful as the United States is not enough for this strong Canadian race. We witnessed what happened when the Fordney-McCumber tariff, the Haw-ley-Smoot tariff and the various revenue bills were passed in the United States. We may wait for an election to make some change and bring in an agreement, but if I understand the temper of the Canadian people they do not feel disposed to wait as long as that.
With regard to the actions of the United States, in 1932, 1934, 1936 and on May 16, 1938, they passed revenue bills. Did we see Washington sitting back and waiting before passing these bills, for fear of provoking or aggravating the people of Canada? No; the fact is that they passed these bills without hesitation. It is quite true that in 1936 we had the United States-Canada agreement, and the president was given power which permitted some of the excise duties which they had imposed against our products to be cut in half. Let us take one example, however; let us look at what happened in regard to rough lumber. Did they hesitate to put $3 a thousand against rough lumber going into that country? They did not. It is quite true that when the agreement came down they cut that duty in half, but the fact is that a tax of $1.50 per thousand still exists in regard to that commodity. That is only one example. Then there is copper. In 1932 they placed a duty of four cents against copper not only in the raw state, but in all forms right down the line, and that was not changed when they came to make their agreement with us; that four cents still remains. I would ask my maritime friends from Nova Scotia and British Columbia, from the north Pacific and the north Atlantic, where fish oil is produced in greater quantities than in any other part of the civilized world:	Was anything
said about a duty of three cents a pound being imposed against Canadian fish oils in the 1934 United States revenue bill? There was not, and that excise duty still remains. They did not stop to wonder whether they were going to aggravate or provoke Canada when they put through that revenue bill.
In June, 1936, they saw fit to impose, not only against Canada but against the world, an excise duty of three cents on animal fats of all kinds. Did we do anything about that? We did not. That excise duty was imposed, and it had a double-barrelled effect. In the first instance it paralyzed that industry as far as Canada was concerned, and it backed up on the world market a billion pounds of vegetable oils which paralyzed the industry

in England, Canada and elsewhere. Was anything done about it? It is true that a reference was made to our tariff board in December, 1936, but was that board asked to bring down its report? The Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and all hon. members of the house know that between December, 1936, and June, 1938, there was ample opportunity for a report to be brought down and for some action to be taken upon it.
Yet with these revenue bills which have affected the lumbering industry, the mining industry and the agricultural industry, and which also place two and a half cents a gallon against gasoline and half a cent a gallon against crude oil and fuel oil, which is produced in Canada and other countries, what do we find happening within the last two or three weeks in the same United States? We find that they again reaffirm the position they took with regard to the effective period for these import duties and taxes. They did not consult Canada particularly about these particular sections, and by proclamation, by public resolution No. 48 as of June 29, 1937, they were extended to June 30, 1939. They are extended to 1939 on four of our main lines of activity. Did they hold up their session of congress or their activities in Washington in order that they might have an opportunity of making a deal? No. Yet we sit here in a spineless, do nothing sort of way, draw our breath and diraw our pay, while the affairs of Canada to my mind are not given straightforward business administration, regardless of where the chips may fall.
Taxation. We have listened to what you had to say about reduction of taxation during the election campaign and many times since. But the truth of the matter is that you have budgeted to extract more taxation from the Canadian people next year than you have for many years in the past. Where are you going to get this taxation? You still expect to find the sales tax either first or second in the group. The sales tax to my mind, Mr. Speaker, is far too high. It is too heavy on the Canadian people. It taxes from the baby in the cradle to the octogenarian in his casket. It catches them all. I am in accord with a small measure of sales taxation which would catch all the people, but I say that this eight per cent is too high. To my way of thinking it is iniquitously high.
Income tax. This is quite right and quite proper, and I am glad to see it where it is. But I think that it is high enough. Nevertheless, the form of taxation which makes

The Budget-Mr. Harris
work-and it is work that we want in Canada to-day; my friends to the left say we need work and wages

is the taxation which will come into the treasury from the goods of other countries, if the goods of those countries must come here. If the goods do not come in, then give us a chance to produce our own requirements for our home market.
The orientation is all wrong. The sales tax should not be first and the income tax should not be second. Customs and excise revenues should take first place, and particularly in a country such as Canada which has such a strong neighbour to the south. The election budget will probably reduce that tax. Just before you go to an election perhaps you will bring the sales tax down. Yes, and my friends at the summer picnics this year will be saying, "We have brought down the sales tax on building materials." I can imagine them standing on a platform and saying, "This very platform on which I stand has had removed from it the eight per cent sales tax, and that has been done by the Liberal government." And those who exclaim from the housetops will also say, "Every article in this house has been benefited by the removal of the eight per cent sales tax.
Mr. Speaker, they will tell us about the great boon that sales tax removal on construction materials has been to the Canadian people. If that sales tax was a great hardship on the construction industry, then I say it is a great hardship on all other lines of work on which that particular tax takes its full toll. It is a non-work tax. It should foe cut in half forthwith. And my suggestion is that in its place we place excise duties to the same amount against goods coming into Canada. That would tend to relieve the numbers on relief rolls, and give work to many workmen. Tariff by scientific arrangement, business administration and carrying out the fundamentals of tariff protection would make for more production, assist mixed farming, market gardening, the development of our natural products, and would not extract so much money from our people.
What do you do with the money when you get it? You spend a great deal of it right here. The cost of government is too high. Are we, as members of the House of Commons, functioning as we ought? Seriously, are we as members of the house doing the job of work which we undertook, when we were asking the franchise of our people, we were going to do? What have we done in the last five months? Perhaps we have enlarged the field of political patronage and meddled with the railways. Perhaps we have meddled in radio, public works and the civil service.
I am glad the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is in his place in the house. He will remember a time sixteen years ago, when East York had a growing population which reached 100,000 people. He will very well recall that I represented 100,000 people at that time. I said I would represent the
100.000	people in the constituency of East York if you, Mr. Prime Minister would do the same for North York. Of course you could not do it there then, because you had to go outside the province of Ontario to find a seat. But I suggested that you also represent
100.000	people in the House of Commons so that we could cut the membership to one hundred, and so that we might function, go to work and do a proper job.
But no; we still have 245 members. And at the same time the Prime Minister will recall that I said I thought there were too many commissions working at that time. What I said then I repeat to-night. Why has it been necessary to add sixteen commissions in the last two or three years to carry out the work of government? Why cannot we as members of parliament carry on a good deal of that work? Why should it be costing $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 each and every year for commissions to do the job of work for the government, work which you and I and the rest of the members of the house feel that we should do? Commissions are set up politically; why not face that issue? We are as able as they are to do the work. If the commissions cannot be cut out; if the government cannot see its way clear to cut at least half of the commissions, then cut out half the number of members of parliament.
We have had the national employment commission, the wheat marketing commission, the textile commission, the lobster and smelt commission, the veterans' assistance commission, the radio commission, the Dominion-provincial relations commission and the penitentiary reform commission. There has been the suggestion to add another fifty cents to radio fees, and to enlarge the scope of the radio commission. Public opinion does not want an enlargement of the scope of the work they are doing. That is one point which should be given serious consideration. To my mind the fees' system should be cut out entirely. Then, we have the transport or railway commission, the tariff commission, the civil service commission, the board of grain commissioners, the national battlefields commission, the federal district commission, the international joint commission, the international boundaries commission and the national harbours commission.
The Budget-Mr. Harris

No session of parliament seems to be complete unless we have some commissions appointed to do work which your people and my people think they sent us here to do. We must remember how, when the present Prime Minister sat on this opposition side of the house; he talked about government by commission. His favourite topic seemed to be that of government by commission, and on other occasions his favoured topic was government by order in council. On still other occasions he talked about governor general's warrants.
The distribution of work which would be effected and the amount of money which could be saved by taking work from commissions and giving it to the members would be very considerable. I shall not go into details, but it was interesting to note the answers to questions asked by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman) with respect to the cost of commissions. I noted the answers given to the questions of my dear late friend, the late member for Waterloo South (Mr. Edwards), and the answers given to the questions of the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mr. Casselman). The answer to those questions should receive the serious consideration of every hon. member, and particularly the government.
Throughout my remarks I have been trying to enunciate principles which would make for more work for our Canadian people. So, when I voice my views with respect to the railways, I have fixed firmly in my mind the idea that nothing should be done which would take railway men from their vocations. To my idea we do not go far enough when we speak of transportation. We speak only in terms of our nationally owned railways on the one hand the privately owned system on the other. When we go deeper into this problem we realize that we must consider the effect of the present trend to ride and carry freight on rubber. We must consider the cost of transporting freight and passengers over our highways as compared with the cost of maintaining our railways. I know this may be under provincial jurisdiction, but I charge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) to give some consideration to the capital cost of our highway system. We should consider this matter in all the provinces. We must take into account the revenue received from gasoline taxes and motor licences, balance the highway budget and see what deficit we have. When we are considering our railway problem we must not forget these three things.
Our railway system has been refinanced and is still being refinanced. There is unemployed money, yes, but the deficits accumulate and

we require more and more of this unemployed money with which to pay these deficits. The first responsibility of the management of this road should be to get a balanced budget. They should have the fullest cooperation of whatever government is in power in trying to achieve that end. We should not put out a budget containing a hundred or more items of expense, and then have the management imbued with the idea that their job is to spend all of the budget allotted to them. A businesslike administration of the road would bring it into a better position, but at the same time the Canadian government and those charged with responsibility should see that it is not placed in an unfair position as compared with highway transportation by bus and truck.
Maturing obligations have to be met. I know the Minister of Finance would not be guilty of bragging of the great saving the Liberal party has made because of his ability to borrow money at such low rates of interest. However, let me say to those who sit about him that it is easy to raise money when so much money is unemployed. There is plenty of money available at low rates of interest. It is quite easy to make the statement that Canada has been saved millions of dollars by lower interest rates; but I ask hon. members this question: How much was that railway debt which has been refinanced worth before the name "Canada" was placed on the back of the bonds? In May of this year the Minister of Finance received authority to borrow another $200,000,000. There was one issue of $916,000 of the Rail and River Coal Company which previously paid five per cent. This was refinanced, with Canada's name on the bond, at a little over two per cent, and it may be contended that Canada has been saved three per cent in interest. When my Liberal friends feel inclined, on platforms throughout the country, to make this statement about, interest being saved, let me say to them that no credit is due for the fact that this government has been able to borrow money at lower rates of interest. That is only the ordinary common business sense which was first shown in the administration of our affairs by the Conservative government and which has been followed by the present incumbent of the office of Minister of Finance.
The Liberal party is the great party that was going to make for unity in Canada. I can remember when their leaders one after another stood up in the Maple Leaf Gardens at Toronto and asked the people to vote Liberal and get unity. What empty words when considered in the light of what has

The Budget-Mr. Duffus
happened since! Vote Liberal and get action ! What empty words in the light of what has happened since! Who are these men of whom we make mention? They are the stand-patters, the free traders, the protectionists, the crack-pot financiers, the monetary reformers, the sound-money men; they are the men from whom the people of Canada expected to get some action. But we have had no action. All we have had is five months of do nothing.
This budget does not help our particular situation. The people of Canada have been greatly disappointed at what has happened during the last five months.
I agree with the hon. minister when he says that we need toleration in this country. I realize that we need goodwill. I opened my remarks along those lines, and I shall close them in the same way. We need cooperation; but, above all, Canada needs leadership and action from her public men in order to have that progress which is necessary to this most vigorous of units that civilization presently knows.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in asking the indulgence of the house at this time, after listening to the speeches delivered to-day in the chamber, I am motivated by a compelling sense of duty to the government, to the people of the constituency which I have the honour to represent and of the Dominion of Canada in general. I realize fully that the budget affects fundamentally the very vitals of the social, industrial and economic life of this nation, and similarly, though perhaps to a lesser degree, that of the other great nations of the world. If I may judge from press reports and from personal observations, it is quite apparent that the budget has been exceptionally well received and likewise well sustained. It is a budget of a Minister of Finance who for two years has been trying to find a way out of an almost insurmountable economic muddle. Having regard to the crop failures of last year and the drought in western Canada with the resultant relief costs, and considering the reduced transportation revenue, he has admirably accomplished his task. As usual, the budget was presented with implicit confidence by a great statesman who has the courage of his convictions and the determination to keep faith with the people to whom he is responsible. At this time I wish to tender to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) my sincere congratulations upon having done this house and the country, by the presentation to parliament of this his third budget, a service that is destined to be an historic triumph.
The minister always discusses economic questions with all that rare insight, vision, thoroughness and power of expression which have led the world to acclaim him as one of the foremost geniuses of his time on monetary topics. His tireless energy, his deep sincerity and his unflagging zeal on behalf of the people of Canada, whose interest he has faithfully endeavoured to serve, have won for him their confidence and their hearts to a degree hitherto not exceeded in this land. No words that I could use would exaggerate what I conceive to be the importance of this budget in relation to the economic structure of the Dominion of Canada. Beyond doubt, it involves Canada's most important problems, and its adoption will bring happiness and renewed confidence to the people of Canada. On account of the vast area of this dominion, it is extremely difficult to arrive at decisions and policies that will be wholly satisfactory to the people in the east, in the west and in the central portion. With our geographical complications it is impossible to please everyone, and unless we have the firm determination to adopt a policy of conciliation, it will mean the eventual disruption of the country.
I am fully aware that changes cannot be effected without disadvantage to some special interests. Governments cannot move far without incurring disfavour in some quarters. In framing a policy in the interests of our farmers, our industrialists, our workers and the great masses of the consuming public, it is only reasonable to assume that some will be adversely affected in certain respects.
However, I am convinced, in these difficult times, when it is the duty of everyone to make sacrifices on behalf of the Canadian citizens, that, when necessary, our industrialists will loyally cooperate with the Minister of Finance and with the tariff advisory board in adjusting their problems in a manner that will bring about satisfaction to a marked degree, especially since nearly every manufacturing concern in Canada has enjoyed two years of almost unprecedented prosperity, having last year contributed to the national wealth the largest amount since 1929. I am one who believes that due consideration should be given to our manufacturing industries to enable them to obtain reasonable profits, to pay fair wages to their employees and to make possible the establishing of satisfactory prices to the consuming public, and that commodity prices should be based always on a study and appreciation of the purchasing power of the masses in order that they may be able to maintain and enjoy a decent standard of living tc which they are justly entitled.
The Budget-Mr. Duffm

Let us not overlook the fact that for years our citizens have been burdened down with an almost intolerable load of taxation. We have administered relief to an extent which almost suggests that the time is fast approaching when we shall have to consider a relief program for the taxpayers of this country if a sit-down strike by them is to be averted. Permit me to say that there is a prudential limit to all spending policies and that the country cannot bear indefinitely an increasing burden. Every million dollars added to the huge debt of Canada overshadows and obscures the wonderful prospect of prosperity and happiness that this land once possessed. We must eliminate extravagance and waste. Municipal insolvency, provincial insolvency and federal insolvency are the triple perilous conditions which have already reached disheartening proportions. Only balanced budgets and a gradual decrease in debt and taxation will save our country from economic disaster. Governing bodies must continue, for years to come, to pare wherever possible and, indeed, even where it seems impossible, with consistent and wise judgment in economic requirements. It is most essential that a policy of pay-as-you-go and if you cannot pay don't go, be maintained. Unrestricted and reckless extravagance and continual balances on the wrong side of the ledger will lead to one thing and one thing only, namely economic disaster.
Present national circumstances demand the greatest concept of loyalty to the state. There should be a total absence of bitter criticism for party purposes. If ever there was a time when the politicians of Canada should forget party rivalry and bend their efforts to serve this country, that time is now. United action, supported by the strength and good will of all classes of people, is most essential to the national progress. Members of parliament and others should not forget but should realize always that governments have no source of income but from the people. There is a general feeling throughout the country that this government recognizes this fact and that it has a sincere desire to lessen the burdens of the taxpayers. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the very high regard that this government has for its pledges, for the sanctity of its spoken and written word, as evidenced by the implementation of its obligations, and by its loyalty and devotion to all interests in Canada, is something of which this house might well be proud. No government hitherto in this country has so successfully and scientifically grappled with the problems confronting it. I think it can

fairly be said that in the history of Canada no government has enjoyed more fully the confidence of the people.
The Minister of Finance has still a very difficult and trying task ahead of him, one that might well challenge even the biggest statesman. Let us assist him to accomplish it. Bitter criticism at this time cannot help. Il may hinder. Whatever degree of wisdom may mark a minister's judgment can only be lessened by partisan nagging, squabbling and bitter criticism. Creating in the minds of the people loopholes of imperfection will get us nowhere, whereas working in a spirit of confidence and cooperation will greatly assist.
All citizens are shareholders in the business of Canada. The eyes of the nation are on her chosen representatives, who are being depended upon to safeguard her interests. We are Canada's board of directors. Let us hand to the Minister of Finance all the help that reasonable fair play and common sense can suggest in continuing his onerous labours. The feeling of the nation at the present time is against playing politics and putting petty obstacles in his way. There is a nation-wide demand that he be accorded every assistance, encouragement and a clear field in which to accomplish the success the country hopes he will achieve, namely, a gradual reduction in taxation and debt and a happy, prosperous and contented nation. If he succeeds-and I confidently believe he will-he may be well termed a superman.
Judicious economies are imperative during periods of economic storm and distress. Great progressive private corporations in many countries have shown no lack of courage in this regard, and they are seemingly emerging successfully, notwithstanding the great burden of taxation, increased as it has been by almost every unit of government. Cooperation by the various governments in the field of expenditure in order to eliminate overlapping and duplication would effect much needed economies. Adequate control and a gradual reduction of relief expenditure amounting approximately to $100,000,000 annually must be implemented on a satisfactory basis. Canadian relief recipients generally are praying to get off relief.
One of the foremost tasks ahead of us is the lessening of the economic strain existing in the various parts of the dominion. The adjustment of financial and constitutional relations between the provinces and the dominion is an immediate problem. The countries constituting the British Commonwealth of Nations have a definite responsibility to join with other nations in reducing all barriers to international

The Budget-Mr. Duffus
trade. This government has put forth a concerted effort to broaden and to deepen the channels of trade, and in no instance has it caused an increase of duties against any country. This policy has contributed not only to the revival of trade but to the removal of international friction and conflict.
The United Kingdom trade agreement, which was presented to the dominion parliament in 1937, assured Canadian farm products a free entry into the British market. In 1935 the total trade of Canada was $1,-
389,000,000, and in 1936 it was $1,663,000,000. In 1937 it reached a total of $1,934,000,000, or an increase of 39 per cent over 1935. The favourable visible balance of trade for the calendar year 1937 enabled Canada for the first time since 1921 to regain her position as the fourth exporting nation of the world, the figures amounting to $1,125,000,000. I quote the words of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) as reported at page 24 of Hansard of this year:
I should like to say how much I rejoice, as do those who are associated with me, in the gratifying progress of this country during the last twelve months.
The year 1937 in every respect was Canada's banner year of hog production. The average quality was better than ever before. The quantity was much larger than in any year except during the war. What is most important is that Canada has at the present time more firmly entrenched herself as the source of supply of bacon for the British market than at any previous time.
The United States provides a market for more than one-third of our exportable products, exclusive of gold an'd the tourist trade. Canada's business with the United States in 1935 amounted to $671,000,000 and in 1936. to $775,000,000; whereas in 1937 it reached the unparalleled sum of $961,000,000. Had the United States-Canada treaty been in effect during the past twenty-seven years, on the basis of the great increase in the trade of the dominion during the past year with that country, Canada might have doubled her population during that period. Anything like trade hostilities between two great neighbouring nations would be, and indeed has been, regrettable and mutually injurious. A policy of good will and of mutual understanding will continue to increase the trade between the two peoples who are both excellent customers, one of the other, and who can each profit by wise and discriminating exchange of business.
According to the statistics of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, 245,000 head of cattle were exported to the United States in 1937, as against 199,000 in 1935, an increase
of 23 T per cent in number and 58-8 per cent in value. The exports of dairy cattle to the United States in 1937, and in 1936 as well, were 7,000 head each year, but the value in 1937 was $425,000 as compared with $352,000 in 1936, or an increase of 7-8 per cent. Incidentally, from January 1 of this year to the end of April, 11,069 head of cattle weighing 700 pounds or over were shipped to the United Kingdom as compared with 688 head in the corresponding period of 1937.
Exports of hay to the United States in 1937 amounted to 144,000 tons valued at $1,069,000, whereas in 1936 shipments were 70,500 tons valued at only $540,000. These items are approximate.
I have here a table showing the comparative increase in exports to the United States in the years 1936 and 1937 which with the consent of the house I wish to place on Hansard.
