The encouragement of tourist trade with the United States by every legitimate means is of national economic benefit. It is of inestimable value in strengthening and increasing the friendship that exists between the two great nations on the north American continent. Uncle Sam's tourist dollar is the thing that Canadians should make a bid for, and we could obtain these tourist dollars in increasing volume by courtesy, fair treatment and judicious advertising, which would mean an icrease in trade and the infusion of new money into the dominion. It therefore behooves us as good Canadians to hold out to them the hand of fellowship, to give them welcome and make them feel at home. Our visitors of today may be our neighbours of to-morrow. It is gratifying to know, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, that Canada's tourist
The Budget-Mr. Duff us

trade last year amounted to $325,000,000 as compared with $255,000,000 in 1936. While I am unalterably opposed to the country going further into debt, money properly expended on the construction of additional highways and feeder roads for the expansion of tourist travel, to increase tourist and other revenues, would be one exception.
Canada is now one of the leading mining countries of the world. Minerals constitute one of the most important resources of the dominion. The progress is amazing, as shown by the 1937 output of $456,000,000, the largest production on record, and an increase of about 26-2 per cent over 1936. In the same year $17,000,000 was paid out in salaries and wages. Another remarkable feature is that in 1936 over $81,113,000 was distributed in dividends. In 1937 the distribution of dividends increased to jver $105,000,000, an increase of 29 per cent, all of which creates buying power for other commodities and thereby adding to employment. The budget provision of 1936 for the assistance of new mines, by which they were given three years to get under way before the corporation tax was collected, has been a substantial inducement to the establishment of new mines and mills. Something like sixty new Canadian gold mines have reached the mill stage under this legislation, and many more are progressing with confidence and increasing success. All this has been a great stimulus to Canadian gold production, which has been the country's mainstay during the depression period. Last year the output of precious metals reached a value of $143,000,000. Prospects are that this year this production will increase to over $160,000,000.
For years the government has taken consistent steps towards reducing the cost of the implements and instruments of production Prices of farm products and manufactured goods were on a par in November, 1937, for the first time in many years. Emphatically we must not retard production, thereby increasing unemployment and affecting income and making progress impossible. Fundamentally industry is our way out. We have to depend in large measure upon the wealth which industry creates and the employment which it provides to bring prosperity to both our workers and employers. Business not only creates wealth and employment but distributes wealth; it is the only sound way in which wealth can be distributed. Industrial expansion causes an increase in the consumption of agricultural products; the greater the increase in industrial areas, the better will be the home market for' these goods.

It is, however, conceivable, even admitting the increasing importance of secondary industry to this country, that we cannot cure the plight of agriculture through the medium of high tariffs. While it is most essential that we do nothing that would detrimentally affect industry, either large or small, it is just as important that we give increased and effective support and encouragement to those engaged in agriculture, for the obvious reason that *farm incomes are inadequate. Agriculture and industry are complementary and interdependent. Each contributes to the other, and what helps or injures one helps or injures the other. But both are indispensable to the solution of our relief problem and that of railway debts and a balanced budget. Agriculture is the lifeblood of our Canadian railways. The public will gladly cooperate with any sound movement on the part of agriculture that is for the good of industry, knowing that prosperous rural communities are essential to the progress and prosperity of towns and cities.
There are two main objects in the work and service of the dominion Department of Agriculture, namely better agriculture and better marketing. Each is linked with the other. It is to this end that the services of the department are directed. It is comforting to know that the government proposes to give the farmers of Canada greater assistance in producing and marketing their products. For example, during the last two or three years the live stock branch has been responsible for the inauguration of some twenty-six organizations throughout Ontario which handle eggs and poultry on a basis of grades. This business is done at minimum cost. The farmer who brings his product to these organizations knows that he is going to be paid for it on a graded basis, and that the grade he gets at the grading station will be accepted in any market. It is estimated that this has resulted in an increase of three cents a dozen to the farmers who deliver eggs to these organizations, and a corresponding increase in other graded products.
In the interest of public welfare, referring specifically to public health, all governments have placed rather formidable obligations on the live stock and dairy farmer. To begin with, we notify him, then exhort him, and finally force him, indirectly at least, to have his herds tuberculin tested, and demand the destruction of diseased animals and subsequent reactors. It is true he receives some compensation, but not commensurate with the loss he sustains. Subsequently he was called upon to follow the same procedure in

The Budget-Mr. Dufjus
respect of Bang's disease, with the same expensive results; and we are now asking him to have his herds blood tested. While not disputing the necessity for this procedure in the interest of the consuming public, I believe the expense is beyond the farmer's ability to pay, and that he is entitled to greater consideration in this regard.
Furthermore, while admitting that governments are assisting farmers greatly in inspection, grading, etc., I submit that we should put forth a greater effort to provide still better facilities of a scientific kind during these critical and rapidly changing times. Improvements in live stock breeding, better and more economical feeding methods, the dissemination of information on more profitable marketing, are all present-day governmental responsibilities of vital importance to agriculture. Scientific research reveals that climatic and soil conditions make it necessary, in order to farm profitably, that the farmer be informed as to the best varieties of crops suitable for his particular locality and his potential market. Greater attention to and more expert information on soil management should not be overlooked, as well as such factors as rust and plant diseases which possibly can be successfully grappled with. Unless the soil contains the necessary plant food elements to produce profitable crops, agriculture will not continue to be attractive to the young people. All this should convince the government, notwithstanding the additional expense entailed, that the solution of these problems demands continuous and effective attention. Admitting and appreciating to the full all that this government has done towards the expansion of the marketing of agricultural products, as evidenced by the statistics I have submitted, I maintain that still greater expansion of markets is not only necessary but imperative. Improvement in quality, grading, packing and shipping facilities of all agricultural products, and the determination to guide them aright into the hands of the consumer, wherever he may be, is equally imperative, and a measure towards greater profit in Canada's basic industry.
In my concluding remarks on this allimportant subject of agriculture I desire not only to recommend but to urge the Minister of Finance and the government to give consideration to a mesaure by means of which a farmer with ample security could borrow sufficient money at four per cent per annum to refund and consolidate his debts and purchase his immediate requirements. I cannot conceive of anything that would do more to stimulate the building trade, manufacturing,
employment, transportation and national revenue as well as agriculture.
At this time I wish to make a few observations in regard to our new harbours board set-up. Speaking in this house on March 24, 1936, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) said, as reported at page 1420 of Hansard for that year:
I do not object to the principle of the bill; in fact, I believe if it had been introduced several years ago Canada would have been saved many millions of dollars-
It is interesting to note from the annual report of the national harbours board for the calendar year 1937 that substantial savings have been made, and that likewise there have been noteworthy increases in operating revenue. At page 7 of the report will be found the consolidated income statement for the years 1935, 1936, and 1937, which shows that since 1935 there has been an improvement in operating revenue of approximately $S35,-000, while there has been a decrease in operating and maintenance expenses of approximately $700,000, making a total betterment of $1,535,000 for the benefit of the taxpayers of Canada, which is a substantial saving. Prior to 1936 the annual salaries of the various commissioners aggregated no less than $73,000, and in addition they received automobile allowances amounting to $15,000, making a total of $88,000. The comparative figure under the present board is $30,000 for salaries with no automobile allowance, representing a saving of $58,000.
Further substantial economies are shown in the entertainment expenses of the commissioners and staff, which in 1935 were $18,000, as compared with $1,500 in 1937 a saving of $16,500 in this one item. The travelling expenses of commissioners and staff in 1935 amounted to $24,000, as compared with $7,000 in 1937. Other economies which should not be overlooked include the entire elimination of residence telephones, which formerly cost $2,200; a reduction in the cost of advertising and printing from $52,500 to $14,600; a reduction in donations and contributions from $24,000 in 1935 to nothing in 1937. These items aggregate $185,700. Since the total head office expenses in 1937 amounted to only $130,000, including engineering and central accounting services, it will be seen that the expenses of the board and its headquarters staff can now be met out of the savings I have enumerated, leaving a margin of $55,700 as well. These substantial savings of the new harbours board provide an outstanding example of the business administration of one item of one department of gov-
The Budget-Mr. Brunelle

eminent, and if time permitted one could cite many similar economies representing the shrewd business methods inaugurated by the government in order to save the money of the taxpayers and at the same time improve administrative efficiency.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasant duty to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the exceptionally practical budget speech he recently delivered in this house. In the course of his speech the minister made reference to the unemployment question and showed that there had been some improvement in the general situation. Members of the opposition and of other groups in the house have referred extensively to the same question, but regardless of that fact I intend to confine my remarks to the question of unemployment and relief which for eight years has been, and for some years to come will be, a vital problem.
I need not say that every hon. member is anxious to rid the country of unemployment. It must be admitted, however, that the Canadian people did not know what relief was; that they did not want relief, and that they were above that humiliating position until 1930, when the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and his followers, through pessimism and vain promises, simply invited the people to ask for relief. By doing so, the Conservative party officially established relief and unemployment as a more or less permanent institution. If one considers the utter failure of the Conservative party to carry out the promises made in 1930, one is justified in making the statement that this party has forfeited its right to interfere when the question of unemployment is being discussed.
Before going further, I should like to say that when the right hon. leader of the opposition recently stated in the house that another crisis was soon coming he did considerable harm to the country. On account of the high position which he occupies his statement was taken seriously throughout the length and breadth of Canada. Our producers at once became suspicious and in many instances adopted a stand-still policy, to the great detriment of our workmen. I have ascertained personally that the pessimistic and unwise declaration of the right hon. gentleman has done much harm to all classes of our people. Let us take it for granted that unemployment and relief constitute a plague. In this respect each member of the house is justified in saying that something must be or can be done,

providing he can offer some practical suggestion. The problem of unemployment no longer should be used as a political football; there ought to be sincere cooperation between all political parties and all the provinces in a patriotic effort to save our country. Believe me, sir, it is in unemployment that communism, socialism and other such movements find their source and thrive, though I am glad to say that our unemployed are still of sound disposition.
There is no doubt that our conditions have improved since 1935, and the government and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) deserve our felicitations. The employment commission has done good work. The plan to train young people in various branches of industry is due to the initiative of our Minister of Labour, in spite of the fact that leaders of the Quebec government call it the Bilodeau-Rogers plan, as though that were its source.
The improved housing plan which is about to pass the house, whereby our citizens will be exempt from some municipal taxes and sales tax, is highly advantageous. The other project to advance money to municipalities for electric, gas and waterworks is a magnificent one. These projects will help to rid the large cities of their slums, and will improve business in general. Another practical and productive plan would be that of establishing more people on the land. For several years ive have talked a. great deal about the matter, but in reality the only back-to-the-land movement has been that of taking the normal number of dead people to the graveyard. I speak subject to correction, but it is my impression that about 54 per cent of our present population is urban and only 46 per cent rural. This is an abnormal condition in a country such as Canada, which is considered an agricultural country. Yet we know that many ex-farmers who are now living in the cities cannot find work. We know they will not be able to find work, as the work is not there to be had. We know that modern machinery will to a greater and greater extent take care of the work to be done.
I would say again to the Minister of Labour that one remedy for unemployment, among others, would be to locate good agricultural, unsettled and unimproved lands, and to open them for colonization. Such lands could be easily located. However, to make colonization attractive, I say each homestead should to some extent be improved at the expense of the government. This would be a self-liquidating expenditure, and would bring relief to the cities. To-day many people are sorry they left the farms. They would gladly return,

The Budget-Mr. Brunelle
but we must admit that such people are no longer fit to do that type of pioneering work which was done by our forefathers.
Let us pay our unemployed men to do the work of clearing and breaking the land, putting up decent houses and barns on each new farm. Those who would take these modestly improved farms would find them attractive and sufficiently remunerative to make them wish to remain on them. Grants and subsidies to homesteaders are not the best form of help, because they resemble relief. We must get rid of relief. Had we used only 50 per cent of the general relief expenditures since 1930 in so improving new lands, and thus creating new parishes and towns, undoubtedly Canada would have acquired a vast additional asset and the cities would have been relieved of a great burden. Let us do it now; better late than never. A colonization plan may be a provincial matter, so I suggest we invite provincial governments to cooperate. Some provincial governments talk so much about cooperation that they have no time left actually to cooperate.
Another measure for the relief of unemployment would be that of taking some steps to reopen those industrial plants which, on account of disastrous Tory policies, closed their doors between 1930 and 1935. There is one such closed plant in Cap de la Madeleine, the city in which I live. In that city is an industrious and thrifty population, the best in the country. They long for the reopening of the St. Maurice Paper company mill, which ceased to operate in 1932, when the then Prime Minister was blasting his way to the world markets. That mill still remains closed, while the premier of Quebec celebrates with great pomp the opening of a new paper mill at Comeau Bay. Again I say the provincial government has a certain control over and connection with such corporation. Let us again ask the provincial government to bend its energies not towards developing political quarrels and idle criticism, but upon finding work for the unemployed, permanent work, and not that which is temporary, unsteady and unproductive.
A further good and practical move would be to reform or to abolish the senate, and thus save money. Let us discard that useless and expensive chamber. Possibly it could be converted into an industrial, practical Canadian chamber of commerce, the functions of which would be to invite and to bring in new industries to our rich country, and to find ways and means of reopening the closed ones. I realize the question of unemployment is a serious and difficult one, but its solution is not beyond our powers. There must be union, harmony, cooperation and
sincerity of purpose between the provinces and the central government.
Moved by a sense of narrow provincialism and by personal ambitions, some bombastic provincial heroes do not hesitate to set province against province and section against section, with the result that the very foundations of our confederation are presently shaken. The personal importance and actual weight of those destructive agents are not extraordinary, but the position they hold makes the condition much more serious. No matter what importance may be attached to the actual causes of discord, their effect upon Canadian unity may be tremendous. It is time that the serious people of all parties should rise against sectionalism. To treat with contempt the anti-national attitude of some provincial premiers is no longer advisable or wise, and I say that a mere passive attitude if prolonged may have serious consequences. Let us remember that there is not always a measure of proportion between cause and effect. Let us remember that the kick of an insignificant cow caused almost the entire destruction of the city of Chicago some years ago.
According to the British North America Act unemployment is a provincial matter. Unemployment insurance is in the same position. Let the provinces settle those questions. However, if they cannot do so, let them step out of the way and permit the federal government to act freely. It is a shame and a crime that the unemployed and the whole of the labouring class should be deprived of the benefits of unemployment insurance on account of the narrow-minded views of a couple of provincial premiers. Provincial autonomy means as much to me as to anyone, but the welfare of the whole country should be the supreme law. Real Canadians and real statesmen do see beyond provincial frontiers. Canadian workmen want unemployment insurance, and it is only fair that they should have it. Had we established such a system of insurance before the last depression, our unemployment difficulties would not be half as great as they are going to be.
It is time that the demands of our labouring classes were met in order that we may avoid labour troubles in the future. Our country will fare better when all classes of the community are organized and united and when their unions are equitably protected by law. Our farmers and our workmen should be united. The right kind of unions protected by the right kind of laws will go a long way to alleviate our unemployment troubles. I believe in labour unions, and I believe in the right of organized labour to declare strikes
The Budget-Mr. Brunelle

and to protect itself against strike-breakers. In brief, the workman's right to obtain redress by means of strikes should 'be respected and protected by all governments. .
It is futile to pretend to make strikes legal and lawful and at the same time to permit someone to spoil the purposes of a strike. Whenever legitimate means have been taken by workmen to obtain redress, when sufficient time has been given to the employer to redress the wrongs, then and only then should a strike be allowed to proceed peacefully and effectively. I speak subject to correction, but I understand a New York state law makes it compulsory for workmen to submit their grievances to a board made up of representatives of the employees, the employer and the business men in the particular locality. Ample time is provided for in which to arrive at a compromise. This law might be copied in Canada. A strike is such a tremendously grave measure to be taken that all possible means should be used to avoid such action.
I know the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Labour are giving particular attention to the rights of labour. The employers and the large corporations can always protect themselves, and our particular care should be for the workmen in order to help them to obtain their legitimate demands. I thought it fit to make a few remarks and offer some suggestions in connection with capita! and its relations to labour. I feel that few other problems have the magnitude of this one and deserve as much study and attention. I feel proud to declare myself in sympathy with the least fortunate class of our people who need particularly to be organized and united in order to enjoy their natural rights and prerogatives.
On motion of Mr. Poole the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Dunning the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
